media.title: Statue Turn

tool_config.idea: Find out by turning a child on the spot that a full turn brings the child back to the starting position and a half turn leaves the child facing the opposite way. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the two turns. Only full turns and half turns appear in this tool: no angle names and no fractions of a turn.
tool_config.title: Statue Turn
tool_config.screen: The school playground at morning break, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A ring is painted on the ground in the middle, and on it stands a child with one foot fixed on a mark, shown large from a high viewpoint. A teal start arrow is painted on the ground and shows the way the child faced at the start; it never moves. An orange turning arrow follows the child's face. The child's free foot leaves a trace line on the ring, so a full turn draws a complete circle and a half turn draws a half-moon, as with Ashutosh and Sahana in your maths book. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: a big Turn button (press and hold to turn the child slowly, or drag the child round); a big STATUE! button that freezes the child; a check row under the child with three buttons, Same way as the start, Opposite way and Neither; three bins, Full turn, Half turn and Neither, for four statue picture cards; a row of explanation cards that click into an answer strip; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the child to the start for this card), Reset (restores the whole tool), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a facing label, Facing now: the same way as the start, the opposite way, or neither; a turn label that says Full turn or Half turn only when the child faces the start way or the opposite way; and a card number out of 6.
feedback: While the child turns, the turning arrow follows the child's face and the foot trace draws on the ring.
On STATUE! the tool says where the child faces compared with the start arrow: Same way as the start: that is a full turn. Opposite way: that is a half turn.

Pressing STATUE! when the child faces neither the start way nor the opposite way shows a soft amber note: This child does not face the start way or the opposite way. Turn on until it does, or call it Neither.
A statue card dropped in the wrong bin slides back with a clue, for example: Where does this child face compared with the start arrow? A card in the right bin locks in with a soft chime.

An explanation card that fits clicks into the answer strip. A card that does not fit slides back with a clue such as: Does this card compare the child with the start? The tool never shows the full explanation.
tool_config.done_when: A full turn and a half turn have been made, the four cards are sorted, and the student has built an answer to the opener's question and given an example of a turn.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: turn Ashutosh until he faces the same way as at the start, then press STATUE!. What has his free foot drawn, and what turn is it? Answer: a complete circle, so it is a full turn. He is back at the starting position.

Card 2: turn Sahana until she faces the opposite way from the start arrow, then press STATUE!. What has her free foot drawn, and what turn is it? Answer: a half-moon, so it is a half turn. She faces the opposite way.

Card 3 (practice values): turn a child until the child faces neither the start way nor the opposite way, and press STATUE!. Is it a full turn, a half turn or neither? Answer: neither. The child does not face the start way and does not face the opposite way.

Card 4 (practice values): sort four statue picture cards into Full turn, Half turn and Neither. Card A faces the start way, card B faces the opposite way, card C faces neither the start way nor the opposite way, card D faces the start way. Answer: A and D go to Full turn, B goes to Half turn, C goes to Neither.

Challenge: 'Can you recognise the child in the picture who has made a full turn? Who has made a half turn? How do you know? Discuss in class.' Look at the statue picture of A, B, C and D, then build your answer from the cards. Answer: A made a half turn, because A faces the opposite way. B and C made a full turn, because they face the way they faced at the start. D faces the side, so D made neither. Cards that fit: Face the same way as the start is a full turn; Face the opposite way is a half turn. Your explanation may use your own words.

Challenge: 'Give examples of real-life situations where you observe turns.' Type or pick your examples. Answer: your own examples, such as a door on its hinge, a tap, a hand of a clock or a giant wheel. Your answers may differ. Next stop: the video that names a full turn and a half turn.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the start arrow on the ground. Where was the child facing at the start?
Turn the child and watch the turning arrow. Compare where the child faces now with the start arrow: the same way, the opposite way, or neither?
If the child faces the same way as at the start, it is a full turn. If the child faces the opposite way, it is a half turn.
Turn the child until the child faces the start way for a full turn, or the opposite way for a half turn, and press STATUE!. The foot trace shows a complete circle or a half-moon.

media.instructions_for_student: The student sees that after a full turn a child faces the way the child started, and after a half turn the child faces the opposite way.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Statue Turn
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration (the free first try of the chapter, played right after the Statue story; it asks and shows, and the video that follows names the turns)
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, chapter opening: the Statue game, and Ashutosh and Sahana turning on one spot with one foot fixed (developer only). No book question sits on this tool and no numbers are used; the four picture cards are practice pictures.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that after a full turn a child faces the way the child started, and after a half turn the child faces the opposite way.
- Out of scope: fractions of a turn, quarter turns, angle names, clockwise and anti-clockwise, minutes.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is a school playground seen from above: packed brown earth with a few small stones and a white chalk ring, about 45% of the stage height across, in the middle. Ashutosh stands in the ring, drawn from above: a round black-haired head with a small nose bump that shows where he faces, cream shirt shoulders, brown shorts. His left shoe is planted on a red cross at the centre (the fixed foot); his right shoe is free.
- At the top edge stands the school gate, at the bottom edge a big shady tree, at the right edge a flagpole. A teal arrow is painted on the ground from the centre toward the gate: the way Ashutosh faced at the start. It never moves.
- Instruction line: "Ashutosh turns all the way round. Where will he face? Make a guess."
- The child is invited to tap one of three guess cards above the ring; then the round Turn button pulses.
2. Scene and Objects
- In the guided activities a faint dotted circle lies on the ring so the child can see the whole circle.
- The child on the ring: Ashutosh in Activities 1 and 3, Sahana (cream shirt, brown skirt) in Activity 2; same size and place, about 18% of the stage height. A short orange arrow leaves the nose and always points the way the child faces. The free shoe leaves a thick yellow chalk line on the ring, so the chalk grows from the teal arrow along the ring as the child turns.
- The gate is the start way, the tree is the opposite way, the flagpole is the side.
- Two big round buttons on the stage under the ring: "Turn" on the left and "STATUE!" on the right.
- After STATUE! a read-out under the ring says "Facing now: the gate", "Facing now: the tree" or "Facing now: neither the gate nor the tree".
- Goal chip at the top left of the stage.
3. Main Interaction
- Hold Turn: the child turns slowly the way a clock moves; a full turn takes about 6 seconds. Let go to pause. The orange arrow can also be dragged round the ring, forward or back.
- STATUE! freezes the child; the chalk stays. The child counts as facing the gate or the tree when the arrow points within a finger-width of it.
- Limits: never behind the teal arrow, never past one full turn. When the chalk closes a complete circle and the child faces the gate again, the turn stops by itself with a soft click.
- Reset puts the child back on the teal arrow and wipes the chalk. Retry is free.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset, Next (Next unlocks when the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Turn Ashutosh all the way round, then call STATUE!" Goal chip: "Back to the start". Setup: dotted circle shown, teal arrow glowing. Guess: before turning, the child taps "The gate again", "The tree" or "The flagpole". Do: hold Turn until the chalk closes the circle, press STATUE!. Result: "The gate again" turns green with a bounce; feedback line: "A full turn: the chalk is a complete circle and Ashutosh faces the gate, the way he faced at the start." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Turn Sahana until she faces the tree, then call STATUE!" Goal chip: "The opposite way". Setup: the tree has a soft glow. Guess: the child taps what the chalk will draw: "A complete circle", "A half-moon" or "A tiny curve". Do: hold Turn until the arrow points at the tree, press STATUE!. Result: "A half-moon" turns green; feedback line: "A half turn: the chalk is a half-moon and Sahana faces the tree, the opposite way from the start." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Turn Ashutosh until he faces the flagpole, then call STATUE!" Goal chip: "Neither way". Setup: no dotted circle, no glow. Guess: "Full turn", "Half turn" or "Neither". Do: hold Turn until the arrow points at the flagpole, press STATUE!. Result: "Neither" turns green; feedback line: "Neither: he does not face the gate and does not face the tree, so this is not a full turn and not a half turn." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1: Statue Cards (independent). Goal line: "Drop each picture in the right bin." Goal chip: "4 pictures sorted". Setup: four practice cards numbered 1 to 4, each a small top view of a child with the teal start arrow and the chalk the child drew. Card 1: half-moon, faces the tree. Card 2: complete circle, faces the gate. Card 3: short curve, faces the flagpole. Card 4: half-moon, faces the tree. Bins: "Full turn", "Half turn", "Neither". Guess: the child drops all four cards in bins, then presses Check. Result: cards 1 and 4 turn green in "Half turn", card 2 in "Full turn", card 3 in "Neither"; feedback line: "Card 2 is back facing the gate after a complete circle: a full turn. Cards 1 and 4 face the opposite way: a half turn. Card 3 is neither."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The chalk shows how far the child turned. A complete circle means the child came all the way round and faces the start way again: a full turn brings you back. A half-moon means the child faces the opposite way: a half turn. Any other place is neither.
- Facing the start way counts as a full turn only after going all the way round, which the closed chalk circle proves.
- Rules the child can say: "A full turn brings me back to where I started." "A half turn makes me face the opposite way."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, and the feedback strip gives the one-line why. Wrong: a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line; retry is free and nothing is scored.
- A wrong guess card is judged after the turn: it shakes; feedback line: what the chalk showed, for example "The chalk closed the circle, so Ashutosh is back facing the gate." Then the right card turns green.
- STATUE! before any turning -> "Ashutosh has not turned yet. Hold Turn first." The Turn button pulses.
- Activity 1, STATUE! before the circle closes -> "Not all the way round yet. The chalk circle is still open." The open gap pulses; Turn can be held again.
- Activity 2, STATUE! short of or past the tree -> "Sahana is not facing the tree yet. Does she face the opposite way from the teal arrow?" The tree pulses.
- A card in the wrong bin slides back with "Look at the chalk on this card and where the child faces. Is it the start way, the opposite way, or neither?" The teal arrow on that card pulses.
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "Look at the teal arrow on the ground. Where did the child face at the start?" (2) the teal arrow and the gate glow and a faint ghost child shows the start; on the cards the chalk glows (3) "Hold Turn until the chalk closes the circle for a full turn, or until the child faces the tree for a half turn." For the cards: "Gate and a complete circle is a full turn. The tree is a half turn."
- Edge cases: the child already faces the gate at the start, so facing the gate alone proves nothing; only the closed chalk circle counts as a full turn. Stopping exactly at the tree or the gate is accepted. Holding Turn at the end of the circle does nothing more.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when all four cards sit in the right bins.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A full turn brings you back to where you started." "A half turn makes you face the opposite way." Think and talk: "Where do you see something turn all the way round, or half way round, near you?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: playground ground from above (flat drawing); chalk ring, teal arrow, orange arrow and yellow chalk line (code-drawn); Ashutosh and Sahana from above (2 flat drawings with a nose bump and one planted shoe); school gate, shady tree and flagpole (photo cut-outs); four practice cards (flat top-view drawings with chalk); three bins (code-drawn).
- Language: English, short sentences. No fractions or angle names appear on this tool.

4. Check: a full turn ends where it began, and a half turn ends facing the other way.
Answer: (a): a full turn; (b): a half turn

content.text:
Worked example: A seat on the giant wheel takes 1 half turn and then 2 quarter turns, all in the same direction. What turn is that in all?
1. A half turn is 1/2 of a full turn. Two quarter turns are 2/4, which is 1/2.
2. In all: 1/2 + 2/4 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/2 = 1.
3. 1 is a full turn, so the seat is back at the starting position E.
4. Check: 1 half turn is 2 quarter turns, so the seat made 2 + 2 = 4 quarter turns, and 4 quarter turns make a full turn.
Answer: A full turn, so the seat is back at E

content.text: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position $E$. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ turn.
content.q_figure: A giant wheel with a seat at the top marked E, and Reema standing beside it.
content.question: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a ___ turn.
content.book_number: Reema's Giant Wheel: two half turns
content.question_tex: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position $E$. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ turn.
content.publication_text: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position $E$. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ turn.

content.text:
1. A half turn is $\frac{1}{2}$ of a full turn.
2. Two half turns in the same direction: $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{2} = 1$.
3. $1$ is a full turn, so the seat is back at the starting position $E$.
4. Check: the first half turn takes the seat half way round and the second takes it the rest of the way.
Answer: A full turn, because $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1$.
steps: A half turn is 1/2 of a full turn.

1 is a full turn, so the seat is back at the starting position E.
Check: the first half turn takes the seat half way round and the second takes it the rest of the way.

content.text:
1. A quarter turn is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full turn.
2. Two quarter turns in the same direction: $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{2}{4}$.
3. $\frac{2}{4}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{2}$, because $2 \div 2 = 1$ and $4 \div 2 = 2$.
4. So two quarter turns are a half turn.
5. Check: two quarter turns take the seat half way round, and a half turn is half way round.
Answer: A half turn, because $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$.

media.title: Quarter Turn Check

tool_config.idea: One purpose, the quarter turn as a yardstick, in two clearly separated activities. Activity 1, Halves and quarters (a short recap of the topic before): join half turns and quarter turns on the giant wheel until they make a full turn. Activity 2, Objects that turn: open everyday objects as far as they go and compare their greatest turn with a quarter turn. Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done.
tool_config.title: Quarter Turn Check
tool_config.screen: The school fair at the edge of the playground, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Two big activity tabs sit at the top, Activity 1: The giant wheel and Activity 2: Objects that turn. Only one activity is on screen at a time, and Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done. In Activity 1 the giant wheel fills the scene: its starting seat at the top marked E, large, with a teal start mark at E, an orange curved arrow and a shaded wedge that grow as the wheel turns, and Reema standing beside it. In Activity 2 a wooden table fills the scene with the everyday objects: a clothes clip, a door with a hinge, tongs, scissors and a file cover, each with an opening arm that can be dragged, and a book corner shown as the quarter-turn guide (a square corner marker that sits on the starting arm). An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls in Activity 1: two turn buttons, Half turn and Quarter turn, that turn the wheel that much in the same direction each time they are tapped; Undo, which takes back the last turn; a row of answer cards (a half turn, a full turn). Controls in Activity 2: drag the opening arm as far as it goes (it stops at the object's own limit); a Show guide switch for the quarter-turn guide; three bins, less than a 1/4 turn, 1/4 turn and more than a 1/4 turn, and object cards to drop into them. In both: Check, Hint, Retry (returns the wheel to E or the arm to closed), Reset (restores the activity), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: in Activity 1 the turns joined so far as a sum, for example 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, the total as a fraction of a full turn, and a note when the seat is back at E; in Activity 2 a note that compares the arm with the guide; and a card number, Activity 1 cards 1 to 3 and Activity 2 cards 1 to 4.
feedback: Activity 1: each tap turns the wheel and adds to the sum, for example 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4. When the total reaches 1 the wheel stops with a soft chime and the note: The seat is back at E: a full turn.
Activity 1: a wrong total shows a soft amber note, for example: Two quarter turns are 2/4, which is the same as 1/2. That is a half turn, not a full turn.

Activity 2: when an arm is dragged as far as it goes, the tool shows the wedge it made and says whether it is less than, equal to or more than the guide, for example: This hinge opens wider than the guide: more than a 1/4 turn.
Activity 2: an object card dropped in the wrong bin slides back with a clue, for example: Open it as far as it goes. Is it before, at or after the guide?
An answer card that fits clicks into place. A card that does not fit slides back with a clue. The tool never shows the full answer.
tool_config.done_when: Activity 1 is done when the wheel has been joined to a full turn in two ways and Reema's three questions are answered. Activity 2 is done when the three practice hinges are sorted and the greatest turn of the five objects is ticked.

challenges: Activity 1, card 1 (practice values): tap Half turn once and Quarter turn twice, all in the same direction. What turn is that in all? Answer: 1/2 + 2/4 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, a full turn, and the seat is back at E.
Activity 1, card 2 (practice values): tap Quarter turn three times, then once more. What turn is that in all? Answer: 3/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1, a full turn.

Activity 1, card 3: 'A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a ___ turn. What happens if she takes 2 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn. What happens if she takes 4 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn.' Use the wheel, then pick the answer cards. Answer: a full turn, because 1/2 + 1/2 = 1; a half turn, because 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2; a full turn, because 4/4 = 1.
Activity 2, card 1 (practice values): switch on the guide and drag the arm of practice hinge H until it meets the guide. What is its turn? Answer: a 1/4 turn.

Activity 2, card 2 (practice values): drag the arms of practice hinges K and L as far as they go. Compare each with the guide. Answer: K opens less than the guide, so less than a 1/4 turn. L opens wider than the guide, so more than a 1/4 turn.
Activity 2, card 3 (practice values): drop the three practice object cards, H, K and L, into the three bins. Answer: H goes to 1/4 turn, K to less than a 1/4 turn, L to more than a 1/4 turn.

Activity 2, card 4: 'What is the maximum possible turn in each of these cases? Check and tick.' Open the clothes clip, the door with hinge, the tongs, the scissors and the file cover as far as they go and drop each into less than a 1/4 turn, 1/4 turn or more than a 1/4 turn. Sample answer: clothes clip, less than a 1/4 turn; door with hinge, more than a 1/4 turn; tongs, less than a 1/4 turn; scissors, a 1/4 turn; file cover, more than a 1/4 turn. Your answer may differ for your own objects.

Join the turns one after another in the same direction. How many quarter turns make a half turn, and how many make a full turn? For an object, open it as far as it goes and compare with the guide.
Two half turns are 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, a full turn. Two quarter turns are 2/4 = 1/2, a half turn. Four quarter turns are 4/4 = 1, a full turn.
Tap the turns for this card one at a time and watch the total reach the answer. For an object, drag the arm to its limit and read the note about the guide.

media.instructions_for_student: The student uses a quarter turn, the corner of a book, as a yardstick to say whether the greatest turn of an object is less than, exactly or more than a quarter turn.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Quarter Turn Check
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S6.T6.C16.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, Reema's giant wheel (a short warm-up with practice values only) and the everyday-objects table: clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover, with the half-turn and full-turn questions (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student uses a quarter turn, the corner of a book, as a yardstick to say whether the greatest turn of an object is less than, exactly or more than a quarter turn.
- Out of scope: angle names (right, acute, obtuse), measuring with pieces, fractions other than 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 1, clockwise and anti-clockwise.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is a fair at the edge of the playground. A giant wheel (photo cut-out, 12 coloured seats) fills the middle, about 65% of the stage height. The seat at the top carries a small flag marked "E" and a teal tick on the rim: the starting place. Reema (flat drawing, red kurta, plait) stands at the foot of the wheel.
- Instruction line: "Reema's wheel starts at E. Tap Quarter turn once, then Half turn once."
- Under the wheel two big buttons wait: "Quarter turn" and "Half turn". The child is invited to tap Quarter turn first.
2. Scene and Objects
- Wheel scene (Activities 1 and 2): the wheel always turns in the same direction. A sum strip above the wheel writes each turn, for example "1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4". A small Undo arrow sits beside the buttons.
- Table scene (Activities 3 and 4 and the star challenges): a wooden workbench seen from the front. A book (photo cut-out) stands at the left with its square corner marked by a glowing corner marker, the quarter-turn guide. A practice hinge is two wooden strips joined by a brass hinge (photo cut-out), about 20% of the stage width; the moving strip is the arm and ends in a round handle to drag.
- Star challenge objects (photo cut-outs): clothes clip, small door with hinge in a wall frame, tongs, scissors, file cover. Each arm stops by itself at its own limit with a soft click: clothes clip and tongs short of the corner, scissors exactly at the corner, the door flat against the wall, the file cover flat on the table.
- A "Show guide" switch with two settings, "Corner" and "Straight line", sits at the top right of the table scene. Goal chip at the top left.
3. Main Interaction
- Wheel: tap Quarter turn or Half turn to turn the wheel that much. The sum strip adds each turn; Undo takes back the last turn; the buttons dim at a full turn.
- Table: drag an arm's handle as far as it goes. The guide lays a faint corner (or straight line) on the starting strip. Object cards can be dragged into three bins: "less than a 1/4 turn", "1/4 turn", "more than a 1/4 turn".
- Reset restores the activity. Retry is free.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset, Check (Check becomes Next once the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Tap Quarter turn once and Half turn once. Then bring the seat back to E." Goal chip: "Seat back at E". The strip shows "1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4". Guess: "How many more quarter turns bring the seat back to E?" cards "1", "2", "3". Result: "1" turns green; the child taps Quarter turn; feedback line: "3/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1: a full turn, the seat is back at E." Help: guided (dots at each quarter place, running sum).
- Activity 2 (independent). Goal line: "Tap Quarter turn 3 times. Is the seat back at E?" Goal chip: "3 quarter turns". Guess: "Yes" or "No" before tapping. Result: "No" turns green; feedback line: "1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4: one more quarter turn is needed for a full turn." The child taps once more and the seat returns to E. Help: independent.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Open the hinge as far as it goes. How does it compare with the corner of the book?" Goal chip: "Compare with the corner". Setup: one hinge, arm closed, guide on "Corner". Guess: "Less than the corner", "Exactly to the corner" or "More than the corner". Do: drag the arm to its limit. Result: the arm stops exactly on the corner marker, which glows green,; feedback line: "This hinge opens exactly to the corner: a 1/4 turn." Help: guided.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Sort the three hinges by how far they open." Goal chip: "3 hinges sorted". Setup: three hinges numbered 1 to 3, guide off (the child may switch it on). Hinge 1 stops short of the corner, hinge 2 past it, hinge 3 on it. Guess: the child drops each hinge card in a bin before opening it, then opens it to check; a wrong card slides back. Result: hinge 1 "less than a 1/4 turn", hinge 2 "more than a 1/4 turn", hinge 3 "1/4 turn"; feedback line: "Hinge 1 stops short of the corner, hinge 2 goes past it and hinge 3 stops on it." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1: Objects That Turn. Question: "Write some of the everyday objects that involve turns. For example, taps, ___, ___, ___, ___, and ___." Goal chip: "Fill 5 blanks". Setup: the sentence with "taps" written and five empty slots; a shelf of nine photo cards: door, scissors, bottle lid, clock hand, nut and bolt, giant wheel, ceiling fan, brick, pencil lying flat. The child drags five cards into the slots; any five of the seven turning objects are accepted. Result: the slots turn green; feedback line: "Each of these swings or spins round a fixed point. Your list may differ."
- Star Challenge 2: The Greatest Turn. Question: "What is the maximum possible turn in each of these cases? Check and tick: less than a 1/4 turn, 1/4 turn, or more than a 1/4 turn. (a): Clothes clip; (b): Door with hinge; (c): Tongs; (d): Scissors; (e): File cover". Goal chip: "5 objects ticked". The child opens each object as far as it goes (guide optional) and drops its card in a bin. Result: (a) less than a 1/4 turn; (b) more than a 1/4 turn; (c) less than a 1/4 turn; (d) 1/4 turn; (e) more than a 1/4 turn. Feedback line: "The clip and the tongs stop short of the corner, the scissors stop on it, the door and the file cover go past it. Your own objects may differ a little."
- Star Challenge 3: Half Turn Objects. Question: "Do any of the objects in the table (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) make a half turn? Write their names." Goal chip: "Tap the half turns". Setup: the five objects opened to their limits in a row, the guide set to "Straight line" over each. The child taps every object whose arm reaches the line. Result: door with hinge and file cover turn green; feedback line: "These two open flat, in one straight line: a half turn."
- Star Challenge 4: Full Turn Objects. Question: "Do any of the objects in the table (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) make a full turn? Write their names." Goal chip: "Try all five". The child tries to drag each arm all the way round; each stops. Then the child taps a card: the five names or "None of them". Result: "None of them" turns green; feedback line: "Every one stops before it comes back to where it started: none makes a full turn."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Quarter turns add up: 2 make a half turn and 4 make a full turn, so 3 quarter turns are one quarter short.
- A quarter turn makes a square corner, so it is a yardstick: lay it beside an object that turns and see whether the object opens less, exactly or more.
- A hinge stops where it stops: the door and the file cover can open flat (a half turn), but none of these objects goes all the way round.
- Rule: compare the greatest turn of an object with a quarter turn: less, equal or more.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, and the feedback strip gives the one-line why. Wrong: a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line; retry is free and nothing is scored.
- Activity 2, "Yes" -> "Three quarter turns are not four. Count the quarter turns: one more is needed." The sum strip pulses.
- Activity 1, "2" or "3" -> "The seat has turned 3/4 so far. How many quarters are missing from a full turn?" The 3/4 place and E pulse.
- Thinks a longer arm turns more -> "A long arm and a short arm turn the same amount. Compare the opening with the corner, not the length." The corner marker pulses.
- A brick or a pencil in the list -> "A brick does not swing or spin round a fixed point. Pick something that turns." The card slides back.
- Scissors put in "more than a 1/4 turn" -> "The scissors stop at the corner, not past it." The corner marker pulses.
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "Where does the arm stop? Compare it with the corner of the book." (2) the guide appears on the table, or the quarter places glow on the wheel with the running sum (3) "A quarter turn is the corner. If the arm stops before it, it is less; on it, it is a 1/4 turn; past it, it is more. Four quarter turns make a full turn."
- Edge cases: an arm that stops within an arm's width of the corner counts as "1/4 turn"; a half turn is more than a 1/4 turn; the wheel never goes past one full turn; an arm not opened fully first -> "Open it as far as it goes first."
7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Four quarter turns make a full turn." "A quarter turn is a yardstick: compare an object's turn with a square corner." "Most things stop before a full turn." Think and talk: "Which object in your classroom opens the most? Can you open it past a quarter turn?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: giant wheel with 12 seats and a flag "E"; wooden workbench; book with a square corner; three wooden hinges; clothes clip, small door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover; the nine shelf cards (all photo cut-outs); Reema (flat drawing). Corner marker, straight-line marker, sum strip and bins are code-drawn.
- Language: English, simple. Fractions are written 1/4, 1/2, 3/4.

content.text:
1. Use a quarter turn, the corner of a book, as the guide. Open each object as far as it goes and compare.
2. $(a)$: the clothes clip opens only a little, less than the corner: less than a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn.
3. $(b)$: the door with hinge swings wider than the corner: more than a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn.
4. $(c)$: the tongs open less than the corner: less than a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn.
5. $(d)$: the scissors open about to the corner: a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn.
6. $(e)$: the file cover opens wider than the corner, even flat: more than a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn.
[Image: Everyday Turns: Ans2: solution]
7. Check: these are sample ticks for common objects. Your own objects may differ a little, so check them with the corner of a book.

content.text:
1. A half turn is two quarter turns, so the arm and the start lie in one straight line.
2. A door can swing open until it is flat against the wall: a half turn.
3. A file cover can open until it lies flat on the table: a half turn.
4. A clothes clip, tongs and scissors cannot open that far.
5. Check: only the objects that open flat make a half turn.
Answer: Sample answer: the door with hinge and the file cover. Your answer may differ.

media.title: Straw and Fan Angles

tool_config.idea: Turn one arm away from a fixed arm and name the angle the turn makes: acute for less than a quarter turn, right for a quarter turn, obtuse for more than a quarter and less than a half turn, straight for a half turn, and more than a straight angle for a turn of 3/4.
tool_config.title: Straw and Fan Angles
tool_config.screen: Pragya's desk in the classroom corner, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. In the middle, large, a green straw lies fixed along a teal start line and a yellow straw is joined to it by a paper clip at the corner; the yellow straw turns. A shaded orange wedge between the two straws shows the turn made. Beside the straws sits a paper fan made of folded green paper with an ice cream stick at each end; one stick is fixed and the other turns, and the fan opens like the straws. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the yellow straw (or the loose fan stick) round the clip; a Show guide switch that shows three marks, the quarter turn as a square corner marker, the half turn as a straight line and the three-quarter turn; an Add a turn button that makes the next turn start where the last one stopped; a Switch to fan button; five name cards, acute angle, right angle, obtuse angle, straight angle and more than a straight angle, to tap; Check, Hint, Retry (puts the yellow straw back on the green one), Reset (restores the straws and the fan), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the turn in words, less than 1/4, 1/4, between 1/4 and 1/2, 1/2, 3/4; the name of the angle once the straw stops; and a card number out of 7.
feedback: As the straw turns, the wedge grows and the read-out shows the turn in words. When the straw stops, the name card that fits lights up softly.
A name card that does not fit slides back with a clue, for example: The straw is less than the quarter-turn mark. Is that wider or narrower than a right angle?
With the guide on, the straw snaps lightly to the quarter-turn mark and the half-turn mark, and the tool says, for example: This is exactly a quarter turn: a right angle.
After Add a turn the tool shows the two turns joined as a sum, for example 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, and names the angle they make together.
On the fan the same wedge and names appear, and the tool counts how many different acute and obtuse angles have been shown.
tool_config.done_when: The five practice angles are made and named, the fan shows two acute and two obtuse angles, and the student has answered the question about two acute turns.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: turn the yellow straw a quarter turn from the green one and tap the name card. Answer: a right angle, a square corner.
Card 2: turn the yellow straw less than a quarter turn and tap the name card. Answer: an acute angle, narrower than a right angle.
Card 3: turn the yellow straw more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn and tap the name card. Answer: an obtuse angle, wider than a right angle.

Card 4: turn the yellow straw a quarter turn, press Add a turn, and turn it a quarter turn more. What angle do the two straws make? Answer: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2, a half turn: a straight angle, the two straws lie in one straight line.
Card 5: turn the yellow straw on to a 3/4 turn and tap the name card. Answer: more than a straight angle, because 3/4 is more than 1/2.

Challenge: 'Use your paper fan to show different acute angles and obtuse angles.' Switch to the fan and open it to two acute angles and two obtuse angles; the tool names each one. Answer: any opening less than a quarter turn is acute; any opening more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn is obtuse. Your answer may differ.

Challenge: 'Make an acute turn with the straws or fan. Continue to make another acute turn. Can the two acute turns together make another acute turn?' Use Add a turn after the first turn, try two small turns and then two bigger turns. Answer: sometimes. Two small acute turns together can be acute. Two bigger acute turns together can make a right angle or an obtuse angle.

hint_ladder.text: Which straw is fixed and which one turns? Look at the green straw and the yellow straw.
Compare the turn with the quarter-turn mark: is the yellow straw before the mark, at the mark or past it? Then compare it with the half-turn mark.
Less than a quarter turn is acute. Exactly a quarter turn is right. More than a quarter and less than a half is obtuse. A half turn is a straight angle.
Turn the yellow straw to the mark that fits this card and tap the matching name card. For the two acute turns, add two small turns and read the total.

media.instructions_for_student: The student turns a straw or a fan and names the angle made: acute, right, obtuse, straight, or more than a straight angle, by comparing the turn with a quarter turn and a half turn.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Straw and Fan Angles
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S8.T8.C27.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, Pragya's straws and the paper fan; Let Us Do (a) to (d): fan, notebook house, 5-sided shape, gymnasts (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student turns one arm away from a fixed arm and names the angle it makes by comparing the turn with a quarter turn and a half turn: acute, right, obtuse, straight, or more than a straight angle (3/4 of a turn).
- Out of scope: measuring in eighths, sixths or twelfths, clockwise and anti-clockwise, any angle measure beyond these names.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is Pragya's desk top seen from above. A green striped straw, about 40% of the stage width long, lies along a teal start line. A yellow striped straw is joined to its left end by a silver paper clip (photo cut-outs); the clip is the corner. At first the yellow straw lies on the green one, so no angle shows.
- Instruction line: "Pragya holds the green straw still. Turn the yellow straw a quarter turn." The child is invited to drag its free end.
2. Scene and Objects
- A shaded orange wedge fills the gap between the straws as the yellow straw turns. A read-out beside the clip gives the turn in words, for example "1/4 turn".
- Five name cards under the straws: "acute angle", "right angle", "obtuse angle", "straight angle", "more than a straight angle".
- A "Show guide" switch at the top right lays three marks on the desk: a square corner at the quarter place, a straight line at the half place, a dot at the 3/4 place.
- Two stage buttons: "Add a turn" and "Fan". Fan swaps the straws for a paper fan (photo cut-out: folded green paper, an ice cream stick at each end, one fixed on the start line, one turning); the same wedge and read-out appear.
- Goal chip at the top left of the stage.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the yellow straw (or the loose fan stick) round the clip; with the guide on it snaps lightly to the quarter, half and 3/4 marks. It never turns past 3/4. The child taps a name card to say what the angle is, and the tool confirms.
- Add a turn: the next turn starts where the last one stopped, and the read-out shows the turns joined, for example "1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2".
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset (straw back on the green one), Check (becomes Next when the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Turn the yellow straw to a square corner." Goal chip: "A quarter turn". Guess: before turning, the child taps the name card for a quarter turn. Do: drag; the straw snaps to the corner. Result: "right angle" turns green with a bounce; feedback line: "A quarter turn makes a right angle: it looks like the corner of a book." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Turn the yellow straw a little, less than the square corner." Goal chip: "Less than a quarter turn". Guess: the child taps "acute angle", "right angle" or "obtuse angle". Do: stop short of the corner mark by more than a straw's width. Result: "acute angle" turns green; feedback line: "Less than a quarter turn makes an acute angle: narrower than a right angle." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Turn the yellow straw past the square corner but not to a straight line." Goal chip: "More than 1/4, less than 1/2". Guess: the child taps a name card first. Result: "obtuse angle" turns green; feedback line: "More than a quarter turn and less than a half turn makes an obtuse angle: wider than a right angle." Help: independent (guide off).
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Turn a quarter, press Add a turn, turn a quarter more, then once more." Goal chip: "Two, then three quarter turns". Guess 1, after two quarter turns: "Where will the yellow straw lie?" cards "On the green straw", "At a square corner", "In one straight line with it". Result 1: the last card turns green; feedback line: "1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2: a half turn is a straight angle, and the two straws lie in one line." Guess 2, before the third quarter turn: cards "Less than a straight angle", "A straight angle", "More than a straight angle". Result 2: the last card turns green; feedback line: "1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4: more than a half turn, so more than a straight angle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1: The Fan. Question: "Use your paper fan to show different acute angles and obtuse angles." Goal chip: "2 acute, 2 obtuse". Do: in Fan mode open the fan, tap its name card, and the tool confirms. An opening counts if its stick tips are at least a thumb-width from those already shown. Result: four stars fill; feedback line: "Less than a quarter turn is acute. More than a quarter and less than a half is obtuse. Your openings may differ."
- Star Challenge 2: Two Acute Turns. Question: "Make an acute turn with the straws or fan. Continue to make another acute turn. Can the two acute turns together make another acute turn?" Goal chip: "Try two pairs". Guess: the child taps "Always", "Never" or "Sometimes" first. Do: make an acute turn, press Add a turn, make a second one; the tool shows the total and its name. Try small turns and bigger turns, then tap the answer. Result: "Sometimes" turns green; feedback line: "Two small acute turns can still be acute, but two bigger ones can make a right angle or an obtuse angle."
- Star Challenge 3: The Notebook House. Question: "You might have built houses using the hard covers of notebooks or cardboard pieces. Look at the angles marked in the house. What angles are you able to see in this house? Write your answers as right, acute or obtuse angle. A: ___; B: ___; C: ___; D: ___; E: ___; F: ___; G: ___; H: ___". Goal chip: "Name A to H". Setup: a house of notebook covers (flat drawing) with eight red arcs lettered A to H, drawn so that A is obtuse, B right, C acute, D acute, E acute, F right, G right and H obtuse. The child taps a letter, then "right", "acute" or "obtuse"; a square corner cut-out can be dragged onto any arc. Result: all eight turn green; feedback line: "A and H are obtuse, B, F and G are right, C, D and E are acute: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 angles."
- Star Challenge 4: The 5-sided Shape. Question: "Make a 5-sided shape with 2 right angles, 2 obtuse angles, and 1 acute angle in your notebook." Goal chip: "2 right, 2 obtuse, 1 acute". Setup: a square dot grid, 12 dots across and 10 down. The child taps 5 dots in turn and taps the first dot again to close the shape. Each corner is named as it forms; three counters read "Right 0 of 2", "Obtuse 0 of 2", "Acute 0 of 1". Result: counters full; feedback line: "2 right angles, 2 obtuse angles and 1 acute angle make 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 corners. Your shape may differ." Hint 3 shows a house: from the bottom left dot go 4 squares right, 2 up, 2 left and 4 up, 2 left and 4 down, then 2 down back to the start.
- Star Challenge 5: The Gymnasts. Question: "Look at the angle formation between the legs of these gymnasts. Identify whether the angles are acute, obtuse, right or straight." Goal chip: "Name 5 angles". Setup: five rows, each a flat drawing of a gymnast with legs apart, a small angle drawing (a dot with two arrows) and an empty box. The name cards "acute", "right", "obtuse" and "straight" can be used many times; a square corner can be dragged onto any angle drawing. Result: feedback line: "Top to bottom: acute, right, obtuse, obtuse, straight."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The same turn makes the same angle whatever the length of the arm. Less than a quarter turn is acute; a quarter turn is right; more than a quarter and less than a half is obtuse; a half turn is straight; 3/4 of a turn is more than a straight angle.
- Turns add: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. Two acute turns can make an acute, a right or an obtuse angle, depending on their size. Rule: compare the turn with a quarter turn and a half turn, then name the angle.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, the strip gives the one-line why. Wrong: a red strip, a small shake, one friendly line; retry is free.
- An obtuse angle called acute -> "It is past the square corner, so it is wider than a right angle." The corner marker pulses.
- A half turn called "right angle" or "not an angle" -> "Two quarter turns lie in one straight line: that is a straight angle." The straight line glows.
- A 3/4 turn called straight -> "3/4 is more than 2/4, which is a half turn." The half-turn mark pulses.
- 5-sided shape: a corner pointing inwards -> "This corner points inwards. Make every corner point outwards." Three dots in a line -> "These three dots are in a line: no corner here." Lines that cross -> "The lines cross. Draw a shape that does not cross itself."
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "Which straw is fixed and which one turns? Compare the turn with a quarter turn." (2) the guide marks appear and the quarter mark glows (3) "Short of the quarter mark is acute, on it is right, past it but short of the straight line is obtuse, on the line is straight."
- Longer straw called a bigger angle -> "A longer arm does not make a bigger angle. Look at how far it turned." Two acute turns called "always acute" -> "Try two bigger turns and look at the total." Edge case: a turn within a straw's width of the quarter mark snaps to it.
7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A quarter turn makes a right angle." "Less than a quarter turn is acute, more than a quarter and less than a half is obtuse." "A half turn is a straight angle." Think and talk: "Can you open a door to an acute angle, a right angle and an obtuse angle? Show each one." Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: wooden desk top; green and yellow straws, silver paper clip, paper fan, book corner (photo cut-outs); notebook house with arcs A to H, five gymnasts and five angle drawings (flat drawings). Wedge, guide marks, dot grid and counters are code-drawn.
- Language: English, simple; the angle names are exactly those on the five cards.

modules.module_summary: Full turns and half turns in games, clocks and wheels, halves and quarters that make a full turn, how far everyday things turn, and the right, acute, obtuse and straight angles that a turn makes.

media.title: Turn Disc

tool_config.idea: Measure turns on a disc cut into equal parts, one division at a time: Stage 1 eighths, Stage 2 sixths, Stage 3 twelfths. A turn is always told as a part of a full turn. A stage opens only after the one before is done, and the divisions are never mixed on one disc.
tool_config.title: Turn Disc
tool_config.screen: A craft table in the classroom, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. In the middle, large, lies the tracing-paper disc with fold lines, a straw fixed at its centre and the starting point A marked on the edge, as in your maths book. A teal start mark sits at A and never moves; an orange curved arrow and a shaded wedge grow from A as the straw turns. Three stage tabs sit at the top, Stage 1: Eighths, Stage 2: Sixths and Stage 3: Twelfths; a stage opens when the one before is done, and each stage shows its own disc: 8 equal parts, 6 equal parts or 12 equal parts. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the straw round (it snaps to the fold lines) or press the plus and minus buttons to move it one part at a time; a Show equal names button that writes the equal fractions for the turn (for example 2/8 = 1/4); in Stage 3, a place to drag the 1/12 pieces onto a 1/6 piece; Check, Hint, Retry (puts the straw back on A), Reset (restores the stage), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: parts moved out of the parts in the whole, for example 3 of 8 parts; the turn as a fraction, for example 3/8 turn; the equal names when shown; a note, a full turn, when the straw is back on A; and a card number within the stage.
feedback: The straw moves one fold line at a time, and the read-out says how many parts it has moved out of the parts in the whole, for example 3 of 8 parts, and the turn as a fraction, 3/8 turn.
Show equal names writes the same turn in other ways, for example: 2/8 = 1/4. The tool says why: 2 ÷ 2 = 1 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
A wrong answer shows a soft amber note, for example: A quarter turn is 2 parts of 8, not 4. 4 parts is 4/8, which is a half turn.
When the straw is at 2/8, 4/8 or 6/8 the tool names the turn it matches: 2/8 is the 1/4 turn, 4/8 the 1/2 turn and 6/8 the 3/4 turn. At 8/8 the straw is back on A and the note says: a full turn.
In Stage 3 the tool shows the 1/12 piece laid on the 1/6 piece and counts how many fit.
tool_config.done_when: Stage 1, Stage 2 and Stage 3 are done: turns made on the 8, 6 and 12 part discs, 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2 and 6/8 = 3/4 found, the full turn completed, and half of a 1/6 turn found to be a 1/12 turn.

challenges: Stage 1, card 1 (practice values): with 8 equal parts, turn the straw 3 parts. What turn is it? Answer: a 3/8 turn.
Stage 1, card 2: show a quarter turn on the disc of 8 parts. How many parts is it? Answer: 2 parts, because 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so 2/8 = 1/4.

Stage 1: 'Show a 1/8 turn of the straw. Show a 2/8 turn. Show a 1/4 turn. Show a 3/8 turn.' Then: 'Continue turning by 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, and 8/8. Check when you have completed a 3/4 turn and a full turn.' Answer: 1/8 is 1 part, 2/8 is 2 parts, 1/4 is 2 parts (the same as 2/8), 3/8 is 3 parts. The 3/4 turn is reached at 6/8 and the full turn at 8/8, when the straw is back on A.
Stage 2, card 1: on the disc of 6 equal parts, turn the straw 3 parts. What turn is it? Answer: a 3/6 turn, which is the same as 1/2: a half turn.
Stage 2: 'Show the turns of the straw equal to 1/6, 2/6, and so on until you complete a full circle.' Answer: the straw turns 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6 and 6/6; 6/6 is a full turn, back on A.
Stage 3, card 1: switch to 12 equal parts and lay two 1/12 pieces on a 1/6 piece. How many pieces of 1/12 cover a 1/6 piece? Answer: 2 pieces, because a 1/12 piece is half of a 1/6 piece.

Stage 3: 'Can you guess what turn of the straw will be equal to half of a 1/6 turn? This is the same as a 1/12 turn.' Fold a 1/6 piece in half on the 6-part disc, then check on the 12-part disc. Answer: a 1/12 turn, because 6 × 2 = 12 small parts make the full circle.

Press plus until the read-out shows the parts for this card, then press Show equal names to read the turn.

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Turn Disc
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S10.T10.C40.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (three stages: eighths, sixths, twelfths)
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, the Angle Measuring Tool in eighths, the circle folded into sixths and the 1/12 piece, and Let Us Think question 1, the six circles with the end arrows (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student reads and shows any turn on a disc cut into 8, 6 or 12 equal parts as the parts moved out of the parts in the whole, and sees that 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2, 6/8 = 3/4 and that half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn.
- Out of scope: naming or sorting angles (right, acute, straight), adding fractions with different bottom numbers, drawing angles, clockwise and anti-clockwise, minutes.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is a classroom craft table seen from above. A round tracing-paper disc (photo cut-out), about 55% of the stage height, lies in the middle with 8 equal parts marked by dashed fold lines. A striped drinking straw (photo cut-out) is fixed at the centre by a brass fastener and lies on the starting point A at the right edge, a red dot labelled "A".
- Instruction line: "The straw starts at A. Turn it 3 parts. Guess first."
- The child is invited to tap one of three fraction cards above the disc.
2. Scene and Objects
- The straw turns the way a clock moves, from A. A shaded orange wedge and a curved arrow grow from A to the straw. In guided cards the fold lines are numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on along the rim.
- Stage buttons beside the disc: "−" and "+" move the straw one part back or on; "Equal names" writes the same turn another way, for example "2/8 = 1/4". Dragging also works and snaps to fold lines.
- Read-out under the disc in guided cards: "3 of 8 parts" and "3/8 turn"; "a full turn" when the straw is back on A. Stage 3 adds a tray of 1/12 wedges and a row of 1/6 wedges.
- Goal chip at the top left. Stage pills in the top bar: "Eighths", "Sixths", "Twelfths"; a stage opens when the one before is done.
3. Main Interaction
- Move the straw with "+" and "−" or by dragging. It never goes behind A and never goes past A after one full turn.
- In star challenges the read-outs are hidden until Check. The child's placement is the guess.
- Reset puts the straw back on A for the card. Retry is free.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset, Check (Check becomes Next when the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided, eighths). Goal line: "Turn the straw 3 parts. How much of a full turn is it?" Goal chip: "3 parts of 8". Guess: before turning, the child taps "3/8", "3/5" or "3". Do: press "+" three times or drag. Result: "3/8" turns green with a bounce; feedback line: "3 of the 8 parts: a 3/8 turn." Help: guided (numbers on the fold lines, read-out on).
- Activity 2 (independent, eighths). Goal line: "Turn the straw 3 parts, then 1 part more. How much is that in all?" Goal chip: "3 parts and 1 more". Guess: cards "less than a half turn", "exactly a half turn", "more than a half turn". Result: the middle card turns green; feedback line: "3/8 + 1/8 = 4/8 = 1/2: exactly a half turn, because 4 ÷ 4 = 1 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2."
- Star Challenge 1: Show the Turns. Question: "Show a 1/8 turn of the straw. Show a 2/8 turn. Show a 1/4 turn. Show a 3/8 turn." Goal chip: "4 turns shown". The four turns come one at a time in this order. Result after Check for each: 1 part, 2 parts, 2 parts, 3 parts. Feedback line: "A 1/4 turn is the same place as 2/8, because 8 ÷ 4 = 2 parts."
- Star Challenge 2: Keep Turning. Question: "Continue turning by 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, and 8/8. Check when you have completed a 3/4 turn and a full turn." Goal chip: "3/4 and a full turn". The straw starts at 4 parts and the child steps it on, planting a "3/4 turn" flag and a "Full turn" flag where the straw is at that moment. Result: flags at 6 parts and at 8 parts. Feedback line: "6/8 = 3/4, because 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. At 8/8 the straw is back on A: a full turn."
- Star Challenge 3: Find the Start. Question: "In the following circles, the end points of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns are shown. Draw arrows to show the starting points." Goal chip: "6 starting arrows". Setup: six small discs, two in each of three columns headed "1/2 turn", "1/8 turn", "1/4 turn", each with a fixed red end arrow, a dashed cross and a green dashed arc showing the way a clock moves. Red end arrows: 1/2 column lower right and upper right; 1/8 column right and lower right; 1/4 column upper left and straight down. The child taps a rim point (8 snap points) for each starting arrow. Check swings a straw forward from it by the turn; if it lands on the red arrow the disc turns green. Result: 1/2: upper left and lower left; 1/8: upper right and right; 1/4: lower left and right. Feedback line: "Turn back from the red arrow by the part of a full turn, against the green arc."
- Activity 3 (guided, sixths). Goal line: "Turn the straw 4 parts of the 6. Is it more or less than a half turn?" Goal chip: "4 parts of 6". Guess: cards "less than a half turn", "exactly a half turn", "more than a half turn". Result: the last card turns green; feedback line: "3 parts of 6 is a half turn, 3/6 = 1/2. 4 parts is one part more: a 4/6 turn, more than a half turn." Help: guided (half-turn line glows after the 3rd part).
- Star Challenge 4: Sixths. Question: "Show the turns of the straw equal to 1/6, 2/6, and so on until you complete a full circle." Goal chip: "1/6 to 6/6". The child steps the straw one part at a time and drops the six cards "1/6" to "6/6" on the fold lines. Result: the straw is back on A at 6/6. Feedback line: "3/6 = 1/2 is a half turn. 2/6 = 1/3 and 4/6 = 2/3. At 6/6 the straw is back on A: a full turn."
- Activity 4 (guided, twelfths). Goal line: "Cover 4 pieces of 1/6 with pieces of 1/12." Goal chip: "4 pieces of 1/6". Setup: four wedges of 1/6 and a tray of 1/12 wedges. Guess: "How many pieces of 1/12 will cover all four?" cards "4", "6", "8". Do: drag 1/12 wedges onto the 1/6 wedges. Result: "8" turns green; feedback line: "Each piece of 1/6 needs 2 pieces of 1/12, so 4 × 2 = 8 pieces, and 8/12 = 4/6." Help: guided (the first 1/6 wedge is already covered).
- Star Challenge 5: Half of One Sixth. Question: "Can you guess what turn of the straw will be equal to half of a 1/6 turn?" Goal chip: "Half of 1/6". The child taps "Fold in half" on one 1/6 wedge, picks a card ("1/3", "1/8" or "1/12"), then lays the small wedge on the 12-part disc to check. Result: "1/12" turns green; feedback line: "A 1/6 part cut in half gives 2 small parts, and 6 × 2 = 12 small parts fill the circle: each is a 1/12 turn."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A turn is told as the parts moved out of the parts in the whole disc: 3 of 8 parts is 3/8 of a full turn.
- More equal parts means each part is a smaller turn: 1/8 is smaller than 1/6, and a 1/12 part is half of a 1/6 part.
- The same turn has more than one name: 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2, 6/8 = 3/4, 3/6 = 1/2. When the straw is back on A it has made a full turn: 8/8, 6/6 or 12/12.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, and the feedback strip gives the one-line why. Wrong: a red strip, a small shake, one friendly line; retry is free.
- Mistakes:
  - "3/5" -> "3 parts moved out of 8 parts in the whole disc. The whole is 8, not 5." The parts left over fade out.
  - Bigger bottom number, bigger turn -> "More parts make each part smaller." A 1/8 and a 1/6 wedge flash side by side.
  - A quarter turn at 4 parts -> "A quarter turn is 2 parts of 8, because 8 ÷ 4 = 2."
  - Counting A as part 1 -> "A is the start, not a part. The first part ends at the first fold line."
  - Find the Start done by turning forward -> "Turn back from the red arrow, against the green arc." The arc pulses.
  - "1/3" or "1/8" for half of 1/6 -> "Half of a part is smaller than the part. Count how many small parts fill the circle."
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "How many equal parts does the disc have? Count the parts, not the lines." (2) the parts are numbered and the target place glows (3) "The turn is the parts moved over the parts in the whole: 2 of 8 is 2/8, the same as 1/4."
- Edge cases: 4/8 and 1/2 are the same place on the disc; at 8/8 the straw is back on A: "a full turn". The 1/12 wedge appears only in Stage 3.
7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "3 parts out of the 8 make a 3/8 turn." "2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2, 6/8 = 3/4 and 8/8 is a full turn." "Half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn." Think and talk: "Why is a 1/12 turn smaller than a 1/8 turn?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: classroom craft table; tracing-paper disc with fold lines in three versions (8, 6 and 12 parts); striped straw and brass fastener; tracing-paper wedges for 1/6 and 1/12 (photo cut-outs). Wedge, arc, red arrows, numbers and fraction cards are code-drawn.
- Language: English, simple. Fractions are written 1/8, 1/4, 3/4, 1/6, 1/12.

Let us make our tool to measure turns.
Cut out a circle from a tracing paper and fold it to make 8 equal parts.
Attach a straw to the centre and mark the starting point as shown.
Now, cut out 1/8 part and 2/8 parts of the circle and paste them on a thicker paper or board. Use these as angle measuring tools.

content.text:
Worked example: The straw on the circle with 8 equal parts turns 5 parts, and then 2 more parts in the same direction. What turn is that, and how much more is needed for a full turn?
1. Each part is a 1/8 turn.
2. 5 parts and 2 more parts make 5 + 2 = 7 parts.
3. 7 parts of the 8 make a 7/8 turn.
4. A full turn is 8 parts, and 8 − 7 = 1.
5. So 1 more part, a 1/8 turn, completes the full turn.
6. Check: 5/8 + 2/8 = 7/8, and 7/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1.
Answer: A 7/8 turn; 1 more part, a 1/8 turn, makes a full turn

content.text:
Worked example: How many 1/12 pieces cover a 1/6 piece, a 2/6 piece and a 3/6 piece?
1. A 1/12 piece is half of a 1/6 piece, so 2 pieces of 1/12 cover a 1/6 piece.
2. A 2/6 piece is 2 pieces of 1/6, so it needs 2 × 2 = 4 pieces of 1/12.
3. A 3/6 piece is 3 pieces of 1/6, so it needs 3 × 2 = 6 pieces of 1/12.
4. Check: 3/6 is the same as 1/2, and 6 pieces of 1/12 make 6/12 = 1/2.
Answer: 2 pieces, 4 pieces and 6 pieces of 1/12

content.text: Show a $\frac{1}{8}$ turn of the straw. Show a $\frac{2}{8}$ turn. Show a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn. Show a $\frac{3}{8}$ turn.
content.q_figure: A circle folded into 8 equal parts with a straw at the centre and the starting point A marked on the edge.
content.question: Show a 1/8 turn of the straw. Show a 2/8 turn. Show a 1/4 turn. Show a 3/8 turn.
content.book_number: Angle Measuring Tool: show the turns
content.question_tex: Show a $\frac{1}{8}$ turn of the straw. Show a $\frac{2}{8}$ turn. Show a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn. Show a $\frac{3}{8}$ turn.
content.publication_text: Show a $\frac{1}{8}$ turn of the straw. Show a $\frac{2}{8}$ turn. Show a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn. Show a $\frac{3}{8}$ turn.

content.text:
1. The circle is folded into $8$ equal parts. Each part is a $\frac{1}{8}$ turn.
2. A $\frac{1}{8}$ turn is $1$ part from the starting point $A$.
3. A $\frac{2}{8}$ turn is $2$ parts from $A$.
4. A $\frac{1}{4}$ turn is the same as $\frac{2}{8}$, because $8 \div 4 = 2$ parts. So it is also $2$ parts from $A$.
5. A $\frac{3}{8}$ turn is $3$ parts from $A$.
[Image: Angle Measuring Tool: Ans1: solution]
6. Check: $\frac{1}{8}$, $\frac{2}{8}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$ move the straw $1$, $2$ and $3$ parts, and $\frac{1}{4} = \frac{2}{8}$ lands on the same place as $\frac{2}{8}$.
Answer: $\frac{1}{8}$: $1$ part; $\frac{2}{8}$: $2$ parts; $\frac{1}{4}$: $2$ parts, the same as $\frac{2}{8}$; $\frac{3}{8}$: $3$ parts.
[Image: Angle Measuring Tool: Ans1: solution (continued)]

Answer: The straw turns $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{2}{6}$, $\frac{3}{6}$, $\frac{4}{6}$, $\frac{5}{6}$ and $\frac{6}{6}$; $\frac{6}{6}$ is a full turn.

content.text:
1. A $\frac{1}{6}$ part is folded in half, so it is cut into $2$ equal small parts.
2. The whole circle has $6$ parts of $\frac{1}{6}$, and each is cut into $2$ small parts: $6 \times 2 = 12$ small parts.
3. So each small part is $1$ of $12$ equal parts: a $\frac{1}{12}$ turn.
4. Check: $2$ small parts make $\frac{2}{12} = \frac{1}{6}$.
Answer: A $\frac{1}{12}$ turn.

content.text:
Worked example: An angle is covered exactly by one 1/6 piece and one 1/12 piece laid side by side. What turn does the angle make, and what kind of angle is it?
1. Lay the 1/6 piece on the angle, starting from the first line, and the 1/12 piece next to it.
2. 1/6 is 2 pieces of 1/12, so 1/6 = 2/12.
3. 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12.
4. 3/12 = 1/4, because 3 ÷ 3 = 1 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
5. A 1/4 turn is a right angle.
6. Check: 3 pieces of 1/12 make a quarter turn, and 12 pieces make a full turn.
Answer: A 1/4 turn: a right angle

content.publication_text:
Worked example: An angle is covered exactly by one 1/6 piece and one 1/12 piece laid side by side. What turn does the angle make, and what kind of angle is it?
1. Lay the 1/6 piece on the angle, starting from the first line, and the 1/12 piece next to it.
2. 1/6 is 2 pieces of 1/12, so 1/6 = 2/12.
3. 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12.
4. 3/12 = 1/4, because 3 ÷ 3 = 1 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
5. A 1/4 turn is a right angle.
6. Check: 3 pieces of 1/12 make a quarter turn, and 12 pieces make a full turn.
Answer: A 1/4 turn: a right angle

tool_config.idea: One purpose, the size of an angle as a turn, in two clearly separated activities. Activity 1, Measure (first): guess the turn an angle makes and check it by laying the turn pieces side by side on it, name the angle as acute, right or obtuse, and read the turn an arrow makes. Activity 2, Draw (second): draw a second line to make an angle for a given turn. Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done.
tool_config.title: Angle Check and Draw
tool_config.screen: A craft table with dotted paper, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Two big activity tabs sit at the top, Activity 1: Measure and Activity 2: Draw; only one activity is on screen at a time, and Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done. In the middle, large, is a sheet of dotted paper. In Activity 1 an angle is drawn on it from a dot, two lines meeting at the corner. In Activity 2 a given line with a dot at each end is drawn on it. At the side lies a tray of five wedge pieces cut from the tracing-paper circle, each with its fraction written on it: 1/8, 2/8 (also marked 1/4), 1/6, 2/6 (also marked 1/3) and 1/12, which are the angle measuring tools of your maths book. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls in Activity 1: a guess box with number buttons to type a guess such as 1/6; drag a wedge piece into the angle (it snaps with its point at the corner and its first edge on the first line; the next piece snaps after it); tap a piece to take it back; three name cards, acute, right and obtuse, to tap. Controls in Activity 2: plus and minus buttons that turn a second line by one piece at a time from the given line, and a Draw button that fixes the line. In both: Check, Hint, Retry (clears the pieces or the line on this card), Reset (restores the activity), Undo, Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the pieces laid so far as a sum, for example 1/6 + 1/12; the total as a fraction of a full turn, for example 3/12 = 1/4; in Activity 1 the angle name once it fits; and a card number, Activity 1 cards 1 to 4 and Activity 2 cards 1 to 3.
feedback: Activity 1: laying a piece shows the sum so far, for example 1/6 + 1/12, and the total as a fraction of a full turn. When the pieces fill the angle exactly the tool says: The pieces fit.
Activity 1: if the pieces are too few or too many a soft amber note says so, for example: There is a gap of one 1/12 piece, or: The pieces go past the second line.
Activity 1: the total is compared with 1/4 and 1/2 and the angle is named, for example: 4/12 is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2: obtuse.
Activity 2: the second line turns piece by piece and the shaded wedge grows; Draw fixes it and the tool checks the total against the turn asked.
A guess that is close is accepted with the note: Your guess is near. The pieces say it is exactly 1/6.
tool_config.done_when: Activity 1 is done when the practice angles are checked, the arrow turn is read, and the seven angles of the book are guessed and checked. Activity 2 is done when the two second lines are drawn and the five angles of the book are drawn.

media.instructions_for_student: The student measures an angle by laying turn pieces side by side and adding their fractions, and draws an angle of a given turn by laying the pieces from a given line.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Angle Check and Draw
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S15.T15.C64.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (two clearly separated parts: Check first, Draw second; Draw opens when Check is done)
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, the angle measuring tools (pieces of 1/8, 2/8, 1/6, 2/6 and 1/12 of a circle), Let Us Do questions 4 and 5: draw angles for given turns on given lines, and in a notebook (developer only). The Check activities use practice values only.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student measures an angle by laying turn pieces side by side from its first line and adding their fractions, and draws an angle of a given turn by laying the pieces for that turn from a given line.
- Out of scope: measuring with any tool other than these pieces, adding fractions by adding their bottom numbers, pieces other than 1/8, 2/8, 1/6, 2/6 and 1/12.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is a craft table with a sheet of dotted paper in the middle, about 60% of the stage height. On the paper an angle is drawn from a dot at the left: a first line going right and a second line going up and to the left of it, both about 12 dots long.
- Under the paper a tray holds five tracing-paper wedges drawn to true size, each with its fraction written on it: "1/8", "2/8" (also marked "1/4"), "1/6", "2/6" (also marked "1/3") and "1/12". The tray has unlimited copies.
- Instruction line: "Guess how much of a full turn this angle is. Then check with the pieces."
- The child is invited to tap a guess card, then drag a piece.
2. Scene and Objects
- Guess cards above the paper: "less than 1/4", "exactly 1/4", "more than 1/4". In guided cards a faint square corner marker lies on the paper at the 1/4 place.
- Wedge pieces: a piece drags by its middle; its point snaps to the corner dot and its first edge snaps to the first line, and the next piece snaps after it. Tapping a piece takes it off again.
- Read-out under the paper: the pieces laid, for example "1/4 + 1/12", and the total as a fraction of a full turn when it is a simple one, for example "4/12 = 1/3".
- Draw part: a given line with a dot at each end replaces the angle; a pencil line appears along the outer edge of the last piece.
- Goal chip at the top left of the stage. Pills: "Check" (A1, A2), "Draw" (A3, A4) and the star challenges.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag wedge pieces onto the angle or the given line. Up to 6 pieces on a card, never more than a full turn in all. In Draw cards the child first taps one end of the line to make it the corner (either end is accepted) and drops the first piece on whichever side of the line the child wants.
- Any pieces whose fractions add up exactly to the angle or turn are accepted, for example 3 pieces of 1/12 or one 2/8 piece for 3/12.
- Reset clears the pieces on this card. Retry is free.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset, Check (Check becomes Next when the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided, Check). Goal line: "Lay pieces on the angle to check your guess." Goal chip: "Check the angle". Setup: the angle made by a 1/4 piece and a 1/12 piece, with the quarter marker shown. Guess: before laying pieces, the child taps "less than 1/4", "exactly 1/4" or "more than 1/4". Do: lay the 1/4 piece, then the 1/12 piece. Result: the pieces fit, the card "more than 1/4" turns green; feedback line: "1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3: more than 1/4 and less than 1/2, an obtuse angle." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (independent, Check). Goal line: "Check this angle. Do the long lines make it bigger?" Goal chip: "Check the angle". Setup: an angle covered by two pieces of 1/8, drawn with very long lines; no marker. Guess: the same three cards. Do: lay pieces until they fill the angle. Result: "exactly 1/4" turns green; feedback line: "1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4: a right angle. Long lines do not change the turn." Help: independent.
- Activity 3 (guided, Draw). Goal line: "Draw an angle of a 1/3 turn on this line." Goal chip: "A 1/3 turn". Setup: a slanting line, quarter and half markers on. Guess: before laying a piece, the child taps "one piece", "two pieces" or "three pieces" needed. Do: tap an end, lay the 2/6 piece, and the pencil draws the second line. Result: "one piece" turns green; feedback line: "A 1/3 turn is one piece of 2/6. It is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2: an obtuse angle." Help: guided.
- Activity 4 (independent, Draw). Goal line: "Draw an angle of 1/8 + 1/12 turn on this line." Goal chip: "1/8 + 1/12". Setup: a horizontal line, no markers. Guess: cards "less than 1/4", "exactly 1/4", "more than 1/4". Do: lay a 1/8 piece, then a 1/12 piece. Result: "less than 1/4" turns green; feedback line: "1/12 is smaller than 1/8, so the turn is less than 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4: an acute angle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1: Five Lines. Question: "Draw angles for the given measures of turns using the given lines." Goal chip: "5 angles drawn". Five cards, one at a time with five dots, each showing one given line on dotted paper in the same slant as the line of the question: a vertical line with "1/2 turn", a slanting line with "1/4 turn", a vertical line with "1/8 turn", a slanting line with "1/12 turn", a horizontal line with "1/4 turn". Result for each: 1/2 gives one straight line, 1/4 gives a square corner, 1/8 gives half a square corner, 1/12 gives a narrower angle. Feedback line: "1/2 turn: the two lines make one straight line. 1/4 turn: a square corner. 1/8 is half of 1/4, and 1/12 is narrower still. Your drawings may differ."
- Star Challenge 2: Eight Turns. Question: "Draw the angles formed by the following turns in your notebook. 1/2 turn, 1/4 turn, 2/4 turn, 1/6 turn, 4/6 turn, 3/12 turn, 1/2 + 1/4 turn, and 1/8 + 1/6 turn." Goal chip: "8 angles drawn". Eight cards in the book's order, each with a horizontal first line given. Results: 1/2 and 2/4: a straight angle; 1/4 and 3/12: a right angle; 1/6: acute; 4/6: more than a straight angle; 1/2 + 1/4: more than a straight angle; 1/8 + 1/6: obtuse. Feedback line for the last card: "1/6 is more than 1/8, so the turn is more than 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4. Each piece is less than 1/4, so the turn is less than 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2: an obtuse angle."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Pieces of a circle are rulers for turns: laid side by side from the first line, their fractions add up to the turn, and a piece of 1/6 is the same as 2 pieces of 1/12.
- To draw an angle the child lays the pieces for the turn from the given line and draws along the last edge.
- The length of the lines does not change the angle. Comparing a total with 1/4 and 1/2 tells whether an angle is acute, right, obtuse, straight or more than a straight angle.
- Rule: lay the pieces of the turn from the given line and draw along the last edge.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, and the feedback strip gives the one-line why above.
- Wrong answers: a red strip, a small shake, one friendly line. Retry is free and nothing is scored.
- Mistakes:
  - Too few pieces in Check -> "The pieces stop short of the second line. Look at the gap." The gap pulses.
  - Too many pieces -> "The pieces go past the second line. Take one off." The last piece pulses.
  - Long lines called bigger -> "The lines are longer but the turn is the same. Measure the turn, not the length of the lines." The angle's wedge pulses.
  - Adds the bottom numbers of two different pieces -> "Do not add the bottom numbers. Compare each piece with 1/4 and 1/2." The pieces slide to the 1/4 marker.
  - 1/12 piece thought bigger than 1/8 -> "More parts make each piece smaller: a 1/12 piece is smaller than a 1/8 piece." The two pieces flash side by side.
  - Wrong total in Draw -> "These pieces make a different turn from the one on the card. Add or take away a piece." The read-out pulses.
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "Which piece looks about as wide as the angle? Guess first, then check." (2) the quarter and half markers show, and a faint first piece appears on the angle (3) "Add the fractions of the pieces, using twelfths if you need them: a 1/6 piece is 2 pieces of 1/12. Compare the total with 1/4 and 1/2." In Draw the third hint says "Lay the pieces for the turn from the given line, then draw along the last edge."
- Edge cases: 1/2 turn and 2/4 turn make the same drawing; 3/12 and 1/4 make the same right angle; a turn of 1/2 draws one straight line, and the tool says it is a straight angle. A turn of 1/8 + 1/6 is never added to one number: it is named by comparing with 1/4 and 1/2. Either end of a given line may be the corner.
7. Ending
- Star Challenges 1 and 2 are done when all 13 angles are drawn.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Lay the pieces side by side from the first line, and add their turns." "To draw an angle, lay the pieces for the turn and draw along the last edge." "Longer lines do not make a bigger angle." Think and talk: "How could you draw a 1/4 turn using only pieces of 1/12?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: craft table with a sheet of dotted paper; five tracing-paper wedge cut-outs (1/8, 2/8, 1/6, 2/6, 1/12) drawn to true size, each with its fraction. The dot grid, angles, pencil lines, markers and cards are code-drawn.
- Language: English, simple. Fractions are written 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 1/6, 1/3, 1/12.
