media.teaching_notes: 1. Draw each angle from a line. Turn the line the given part of a full turn. 2. 1/2 turn: a straight angle. 3. 1/4 turn: a right angle. 4. 2/4 turn: 2/4 = 1/2, so it is a straight angle. 5. 1/6 turn: less than a 1/4 turn, so it is an acute angle. 6. 4/6 turn: 4/6 is more than 3/6, and 3/6 is 1/2. So it is more than a straight angle. 7. 3/12 turn: 3/12 = 1/4, a right angle. 8. 1/2 + 1/4 turn: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4, more than 1/2: more than a straight angle. 9. 1/8 + 1/6 turn: 1/6 is more than 1/8, so the total is more than 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4. Each part is less than 1/4, so the total is less than 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. It is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2: an obtuse angle. 10. Check: 2/4 and 1/2 are the same turn, and 3/12 and 1/4 are the same turn. Answer: 1/2 and 2/4: straight; 1/4 and 3/12: right; 1/6: acute; 4/6 and 1/2 + 1/4: more than straight; 1/8 + 1/6: obtuse.

content.text:
1. Draw each angle from a line. Turn the line the given part of a full turn.
2. $\frac{1}{2}$ turn: a straight angle.
3. $\frac{1}{4}$ turn: a right angle.
4. $\frac{2}{4}$ turn: $\frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$, so it is a straight angle.
5. $\frac{1}{6}$ turn: less than a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn, so it is an acute angle.
6. $\frac{4}{6}$ turn: $\frac{4}{6}$ is more than $\frac{3}{6}$, and $\frac{3}{6}$ is $\frac{1}{2}$. So it is more than a straight angle.
[Image: Let us do: Ans2: solution]
7. $\frac{3}{12}$ turn: $\frac{3}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$, a right angle.
8. $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4}$ turn: $\frac{2}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$, more than $\frac{1}{2}$: more than a straight angle.
9. $\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{6}$ turn: $\frac{1}{6}$ is more than $\frac{1}{8}$, so the total is more than $\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$. Each part is less than $\frac{1}{4}$, so the total is less than $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$. It is more than $\frac{1}{4}$ and less than $\frac{1}{2}$: an obtuse angle.
10. Check: $\frac{2}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ are the same turn, and $\frac{3}{12}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$ are the same turn.
Answer: $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{2}{4}$: straight; $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{3}{12}$: right; $\frac{1}{6}$: acute; $\frac{4}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4}$: more than straight; $\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{6}$: obtuse.
[Image: Let us do: Ans2: solution (continued)]

media.title: Minute Hand Turner

tool_config.idea: Link the minutes the minute hand moves to the fraction of a full turn it makes: 60 minutes is a full turn, so 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn, 30 is a 1/2 turn, 45 is a 3/4 turn and 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn, and the hand turns from the place where it starts.
tool_config.title: Minute Hand Turner
tool_config.screen: The clock on the school wall, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The clock face is large and fills the middle of the screen, with the numbers 1 to 12 and a ring of minute marks, and a long minute hand. A teal dot marks the starting place of the hand; an orange shaded sweep grows from the start as the hand turns, and a curved arrow follows the hand in the way a clock moves. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the minute hand the way a clock moves (it snaps to the 5 minute marks, and a Show single minutes switch adds the minute marks between); plus 5 and minus 5 minute buttons; a Start at selector that places the starting dot at any number of the clock; fraction cards, 1/12, 1/6, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 and 3/4, to tap so that the hand turns that part; answer boxes for the turn and for the minutes; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the hand to its starting place), Reset (restores the clock), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: moved by a number of minutes; turn as a fraction of a full turn; the number the hand points at now; and a card number out of 7.
feedback: As the hand moves, the sweep grows and the read-outs show the minutes moved and the turn as a fraction of a full turn, for example 15 minutes, a 1/4 turn.
A wrong turn shows a soft amber note, for example: A full turn is 60 minutes. 15 minutes is 15 × 4 = 60, so it is a 1/4 turn.
The hand always turns from the starting dot, not from 12, and the tool says so, for example: The hand started at 2, so it stops at 7, not at 5.
A fraction card turns the hand that part of a full turn and shows the minutes, for example: 1/12 of 60 minutes is 5 minutes.
When the hand is back on the starting dot the note says: a full turn, 60 minutes.
tool_config.done_when: The five practice cards are done with the turn and the stopping place read correctly, and the student has answered all seven parts of the book's minute hand question.

media.instructions_for_student: The student finds the turn a minute hand makes from the minutes it moves and the minutes from the turn, knowing that 60 minutes is a full turn and 5 minutes is 1/12 of it.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Minute Hand Turner
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S17.T17.C70.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, the minute hand of a clock, and Let Us Do question 6 (a) to (g): the turn for 15, 30 and 45 minutes, and the minutes for turns of 1/12, a full circle, 1/6 and 4/12, with the starting place of the hand given each time (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds the turn a minute hand makes from the minutes it moves and the minutes from the turn, knowing that 60 minutes is a full turn and 5 minutes is 1/12 of it, and finds where the hand stops.
- Out of scope: the hour hand, reading the time, seconds, angles of other shapes, clockwise and anti-clockwise as names.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is the clock on the school wall: a round wall clock (photo cut-out) with a white face, the numbers 1 to 12 and a ring of minute marks, about 70% of the stage height. Only the long minute hand is drawn. A teal dot on the rim marks the place where the hand starts, here at 12.
- Instruction line: "The hand starts at 12. Move it 35 minutes. Guess the turn first."
- The child is invited to tap one of three fraction cards above the clock.
2. Scene and Objects
- Clock with a long black minute hand with a red tip. As the hand moves, an orange shaded sweep grows from the teal dot to the hand and a curved orange arrow follows it, the way a clock moves.
- Stage buttons beside the clock: "−5" and "+5" move the hand 5 minutes back or on. The hand can also be dragged; it snaps to the 5 minute marks.
- Read-outs in guided cards: "Minutes moved: 35", "Pieces of 1/12: 7" and "The hand points at 7". In independent cards the read-outs are hidden until Check.
- Cards: fraction cards "1/12", "1/6", "1/4", "1/3", "1/2", "3/4" for guesses in the activities (the star challenge cards show the options that fit the question); minute cards "1", "5", "10", "12", "20", "30", "60".
- Goal chip at the top left of the stage.
3. Main Interaction
- Move the hand from the teal dot with "+5", "−5" or by dragging. It never goes behind the teal dot and never past one full turn. The hand always moves the way a clock moves.
- Tap a card to guess or to fill in a blank. In the star challenges each clock has its own blank sentence; the child taps the blank, picks a card, then drags the hand to its final place.
- Reset puts the hand back on the teal dot. Retry is free.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset, Check (Check becomes Next when the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Start at 12. Move the hand 35 minutes." Goal chip: "35 minutes". Guess: before moving, the child taps "5/12", "7/12" or "9/12" for the turn. Do: press "+5" seven times or drag. Result: "7/12" turns green with a bounce; feedback line: "35 ÷ 5 = 7 pieces of 1/12, so it is a 7/12 turn. The hand stops at 7." Help: guided (every number shows its minutes, read-outs on).
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Start at 4. Move the hand 40 minutes. Where does it stop?" Goal chip: "40 minutes". Setup: teal dot at 4, the 20 minute mark. Guess: the child taps the number the hand will stop at: "4", "8" or "12". Result: "12" turns green; feedback line: "40 ÷ 5 = 8 pieces of 1/12: an 8/12 turn. The hand starts at 4, the 20 minute mark, and 20 + 40 = 60 brings it to 12." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Start at 8. Move the hand 50 minutes. Where does it stop?" Goal chip: "Past 12". Setup: teal dot at 8, the 40 minute mark; no minute numbers. Guess: cards "2", "6" or "10". Result: "6" turns green; feedback line: "50 ÷ 5 = 10 pieces of 1/12: a 10/12 turn. The hand starts at 8, the 40 minute mark, and 40 + 50 = 90 = 60 + 30: it goes past 12 and stops at 6, the 30 minute mark." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Start at 12. The hand turns 11/12 of a full turn. How many minutes is that?" Goal chip: "11/12 turn". Guess: minute cards "11", "55" or "60". Do: drag the hand 11 numbers round. Result: "55" turns green; feedback line: "11 pieces of 1/12, and 11 × 5 = 55 minutes. The hand stops at 11, one piece short of a full turn." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1: Turns for Minutes. Question: "Guess the measure of turns the minute hand of a clock makes in each of the following cases. The initial position of the minute hand is given. Draw the final position of the minute hand on the clock face. Discuss your reasoning in class. (a): When the minute hand moves by 15 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (b): When the minute hand moves by 30 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (c): When the minute hand moves by 45 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle." Goal chip: "3 clocks done". Setup: three clocks in a row with the hand starting at 3 in (a), 6 in (b) and 9 in (c). The child fills each blank and drags each hand to its final place. Result: (a) 1/4, the hand stops at 6; (b) 1/2, it stops at 12; (c) 3/4, it stops at 6. Feedback line: "15 × 4 = 60 so 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn; 30 × 2 = 60 so 30 minutes is a 1/2 turn; 3 × 15 = 45 so 45 minutes is a 3/4 turn."
- Star Challenge 2: Minutes for Turns. Question: "(d): When the minute hand has turned by 1/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (e): When the minute hand has turned a full-circle, it has moved by ___ minutes. (f): When the minute hand has turned by 1/6 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (g): When the minute hand has turned by 4/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes." Goal chip: "4 clocks done". Setup: four clocks with the hand starting at 1 in (d), at 12 in (e), at 2 in (f) and at 4 in (g). The child fills each blank with a minute card and drags each hand to its final place. Result: (d) 5 minutes, the hand stops at 2; (e) 60 minutes, it stops at 12; (f) 10 minutes, it stops at 4; (g) 20 minutes, it stops at 8. Feedback line: "60 ÷ 12 = 5, so a 1/12 turn is 5 minutes; a full circle is 60; 60 ÷ 6 = 10 for a 1/6 turn; and 4 × 5 = 20 for 4/12."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The minute hand makes a full turn in 60 minutes. Each step from one number to the next is 5 minutes and a 1/12 turn, so minutes ÷ 5 gives the number of pieces of 1/12.
- 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn, 30 a 1/2 turn, 45 a 3/4 turn and 60 a full turn.
- The hand turns from where it starts, not always from 12: the stopping place is the start plus the minutes, taking away 60 when it passes 12.
- Rule: 60 minutes is a full turn, 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn, and the hand turns from where it starts.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, and the feedback strip gives the one-line why above.
- Wrong answers: a red strip, a small shake, one friendly line. Retry is free and nothing is scored.
- Mistakes:
  - Counts the numbers as minutes -> "The hand moved 7 numbers, not 7 minutes. Each number is 5 minutes." The 5 minute marks pulse.
  - Always starts from 12 -> "The hand started at the teal dot, not at 12. Count the minutes from there." The teal dot pulses.
  - 1/12 turn called 12 minutes -> "1/12 of 60 minutes is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes, not 12." The sweep shows one piece of 1/12.
  - 1/6 thought smaller than 1/12 -> "More parts make each part smaller. A 1/6 turn is 10 minutes and a 1/12 turn is 5." Both sweeps flash.
  - Wrong fraction for 15 minutes -> "15 × 4 = 60, so 15 minutes is a quarter of the way round: 1/4." The quarter places glow.
  - Forgets to go past 12 -> "The hand passes 12 and keeps going. Take away 60 from the total." The 12 pulses.
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "Where does the minute hand start? Look at the teal dot, not always at 12." (2) the minute marks (5, 10, 15 and so on) show beside the numbers and the sweep splits into pieces of 1/12 (3) "A full turn is 60 minutes and a 1/12 turn is 5 minutes. Count the 5 minute steps for this card."
- Edge cases: 60 minutes brings the hand back to the teal dot, a full turn; a hand that passes 12 keeps counting; no turn can be more than a full turn; a start at 12 and a stop at 12 after 60 minutes is a full turn, not 0.
7. Ending
- Star Challenges 1 and 2 are done when all seven clocks are right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A full turn of the minute hand is 60 minutes." "A 1/12 turn is 5 minutes, from one number to the next." "The hand turns from where it starts, not always from 12." Think and talk: "The minute hand starts at 9 and turns a half turn. Where does it stop?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: round wall clock face with numbers and minute marks (photo cut-out); minute hand, teal start dot, sweep, curved arrow and cards are code-drawn.
- Language: English, simple. Times are minutes only; fractions are written 1/12, 1/6, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4.

content.text:
1. A full turn of the minute hand is $60$ minutes. A $\frac{1}{12}$ turn is $5$ minutes.
2. $(a)$: $15$ minutes: $15 \times 4 = 60$, so it is a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn. The hand starts at $3$ and stops at $6$.
3. $(b)$: $30$ minutes: $30 \times 2 = 60$, so it is a $\frac{1}{2}$ turn. From $6$ the hand stops at $12$.
4. $(c)$: $45$ minutes: $3 \times 15 = 45$, so it is $3$ quarter turns, a $\frac{3}{4}$ turn. From $9$ the hand stops at $6$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
5. $(d)$: a $\frac{1}{12}$ turn is $60 \div 12 = 5$ minutes. From $1$ the hand stops at $2$.
6. $(e)$: a full circle is $60$ minutes. The hand starts and stops at $12$.
7. $(f)$: a $\frac{1}{6}$ turn is $60 \div 6 = 10$ minutes. From $2$ the hand stops at $4$.
8. $(g)$: a $\frac{4}{12}$ turn is $4 \times 5 = 20$ minutes, because one $\frac{1}{12}$ turn is $60 \div 12 = 5$ minutes. From $4$ the hand stops at $8$.
9. Check: $\frac{4}{12}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{3}$, and $20 \times 3 = 60$.
Answer: $(a)$: $\frac{1}{4}$; $(b)$: $\frac{1}{2}$; $(c)$: $\frac{3}{4}$; $(d)$: $5$; $(e)$: $60$; $(f)$: $10$; $(g)$: $20$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.instructions_for_student: The student finds the direction faced after turns of right angles, clockwise or anti-clockwise, counting one step round the compass for each right angle.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Turn and Face
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S19.T19.C75.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Angles as Turns, Fun with Turns questions 1 (the table) and 2 (Padma and the toy shop) (developer only). Activities 1 to 5 use practice values only.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds the direction faced after turns of right angles, clockwise or anti-clockwise, counting one step round the compass for each right angle.
- Out of scope: angles other than right angles and half right angles, the minute hand, names for the points between the four directions, telling which way a creature or an object turns.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The stage is a compass painted on a playground, seen from above: a ring on grey paving, about 60% of the stage height across. Four wooden signboards (photo cut-outs) stand on it: "NORTH" at the top, "EAST" on the right, "SOUTH" at the bottom, "WEST" on the left. A child stands in the middle (flat drawing from above: round head, nose bump, shirt shoulders) with a short orange arrow showing where the child faces.
- A small wall clock (photo cut-out) in the top right corner has a hand that moves round the way a clock moves.
- Instruction line: "The child faces North. Turn 1 right angle clockwise. Where will the child face?"
- The child is invited to tap a signboard to guess.
2. Scene and Objects
- In guided cards small arrows along the ring show the clockwise order: North, East, South, West.
- Stage buttons under the compass: "Clockwise" and "Anti-clockwise" (a curved arrow on each), "1 right angle", "1/2 right angle" and a small "Undo" arrow.
- Read-out: the turns so far, for example "2 right angles clockwise", and in guided cards "Facing now: South". Goal chip at the top left.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap Clockwise or Anti-clockwise first; it stays lit. Each tap on "1 right angle" turns the child that much; "1/2 right angle" turns half as far, half way between two signs. Undo takes back the last turn. At most 8 turns on a card.
- To answer, the child taps the signboard where the child faces at the end. In the table, the child taps a row, plays the turns and taps a sign to fill the Ending Direction cell.
- Reset puts the child back on the starting sign. Retry is free.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Reset, Check (Check becomes Next when the goal chip is green).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "The child faces North. Turn 1 right angle clockwise, then undo and turn 1 right angle anti-clockwise." Goal chip: "East, then West". Guess: the child taps a signboard for the clockwise turn. Result: "EAST" turns green; feedback line: "Clockwise is the way a clock moves: North, then East. Anti-clockwise is the other way: North, then West." Help: guided (arrows on the ring, the clock moves with the child).
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "The child faces East. Turn 2 right angles clockwise. Then undo and turn 2 right angles anti-clockwise." Goal chip: "A half turn both ways". Guess: "Will both turns end in the same place?" cards "Yes" or "No". Result: "Yes" turns green; feedback line: "East, 2 right angles clockwise: South, then West. Anti-clockwise: North, then West. A half turn ends in the same place either way."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "The child faces West. Turn 1 right angle clockwise, then undo and turn 1 right angle anti-clockwise." Goal chip: "A quarter turn each way". Guess: cards "Same place" or "Different places". Result: "Different places" turns green; feedback line: "West, 1 right angle clockwise: North. Anti-clockwise: South. A quarter turn ends in different places."
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "The child faces South. Turn 3 right angles anti-clockwise. Where does the child face?" Goal chip: "3 right angles anti-clockwise". Guess: the child taps a signboard first. Result: "WEST" turns green; feedback line: "Anti-clockwise from South goes East, North, West: 3 right angles end at West." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (guided). Goal line: "The child faces North. Turn 1/2 right angle clockwise, then 1/2 right angle more." Goal chip: "Two halves". Guess: "How many right angles in all?" cards "1/2", "1" or "2". Result: "1" turns green; feedback line: "1/2 + 1/2 = 1: two half right angles make 1 right angle, so the child faces East." Help: guided (a dot marks the place half way between North and East).
- Star Challenge 1: The Table. Question: "The children in a class are playing a game in which the teacher tells them the direction in which they should rotate. Complete the table by filling the direction the children will face on completing the given turns. The starting direction is given in the table. (a): North, two right angles clockwise; (b): South, two right angles anti-clockwise; (c): East, four right angles anti-clockwise; (d): West, four right angles clockwise; (e): North, 5 right angles clockwise; (f): South, 3 right angles clockwise, 1/2 right angle clockwise, 1/2 right angle clockwise; (g): West, ___ right angles clockwise, four 1/2 right angles anti-clockwise". Goal chip: "7 rows filled". Setup: the compass on the left and the seven-row table on the right, each row with an empty Ending Direction cell. The child guesses by tapping a sign, then plays the row to check. Row (g) has a number stepper (2 to 6) in the blank, because the book prints no number. Result: (a) South; (b) North; (c) East; (d) West; (e) East; (f) South; (g) depends on the number: with 3 it is North. Feedback line: "4 right angles make a full turn: (c), (d) and (f) end where they started. (e): 5 − 4 = 1 right angle clockwise from North is East. (g): four 1/2 right angles are 2 right angles anti-clockwise, so 3 − 2 = 1 right angle clockwise is left: West to North."
- Star Challenge 2: Padma. Question: "Padma is facing the toy shop. What place will she face if she takes a half turn clockwise?" and then "What other way can Padma turn to face the same place?" Goal chip: "Two ways to the same place". Setup: a street map from above: Padma at the centre (flat drawing, yellow top, plait), the toy shop at the top, the parking sign and guard on the right, the bookstall on the left, the ice cream cart at the bottom. Part 1: the child taps the place, then turns Padma a half turn clockwise to check. Part 2: reset, then the child turns Padma another way, for example 2 right angles anti-clockwise. Result: "the ice cream cart" both times. Feedback line: "A half turn is 2 right angles. Clockwise: the parking sign, then the ice cream cart. Anti-clockwise: the bookstall, then the ice cream cart."
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A right angle is a quarter turn, one step to the next sign. Clockwise goes North, East, South, West, North; anti-clockwise goes North, West, South, East, North. 4 right angles bring you back, so 5 is the same as 1.
- A half turn (2 right angles) ends in the same place either way, but a quarter turn does not. Two 1/2 right angles make 1 right angle.
- Rule: count the right angles, move that many signs clockwise or anti-clockwise, and 4 bring you back.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks, and the feedback strip gives the one-line why. Wrong: a red strip, a small shake, one friendly line; retry is free.
- Mistakes:
  - Thinks a half turn differs by direction -> "A half turn ends in the same place either way, but a quarter turn does not." The two end arrows show together.
  - 5 right angles answered with North -> "4 right angles make a full turn and bring you back. 5 is 4 and 1 more." The 4th step pulses.
  - Padma, clockwise half turn answered with the bookstall -> "Clockwise from the toy shop goes to the parking sign first. Take 2 right angles." The first curved arrow shows.
- Hints, 3 levels: (1) "Which way do the hands of a clock go? That is clockwise." (2) arrows on the ring show the clockwise order and the starting sign glows (3) "From the start move one sign for each right angle, the way the card says. 4 right angles bring you back."
- Edge cases: 4 right angles end on the starting sign; 5 is 4 and 1; 3 right angles anti-clockwise end where 1 right angle clockwise ends; the first right angle goes to the next sign, not the starting one; row (g) works for any number from 2 to 6.
7. Ending
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move. Anti-clockwise is the other way." "Each right angle is one step round the compass, and 4 right angles bring you back." "A half turn ends in the same place either way." Think and talk: "You face North. Is 1 right angle clockwise the same as 3 right angles anti-clockwise?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: playground paving with a painted compass ring; four signboards, small wall clock (photo cut-outs); top-view child, Padma, street map with toy shop, bookstall, parking sign with guard and ice cream cart (flat drawings). Arrows, dots and the table are code-drawn.
- Language: English, simple. Direction words are exactly "clockwise" and "anti-clockwise".

content.text:
Worked example: Padma faces West and turns 3 right angles anti-clockwise. Which direction does she face?
1. Anti-clockwise from West, the order is West, South, East, North.
2. 1 right angle anti-clockwise: South.
3. 2 right angles: East.
4. 3 right angles: North.
5. So she faces North.
6. Check: 3 right angles anti-clockwise is the same as 1 right angle clockwise, because 3 + 1 = 4. West turned 1 right angle clockwise is North.

It ends at South. 3. (b): South, 2 right angles anti-clockwise: East, then North. It ends at North. 4. (c): East, 4 right angles anti-clockwise: a full turn, back at East. 5. (d): West, 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at West. 6. (e): North, 5 right angles clockwise: 4 of them are a full turn, and 5 − 4 = 1 more takes it to East. 7. (f): South, 3 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at South. 8. (g): West. Four 1/2 right angles are 2 right angles anti-clockwise. The number before 'right angles clockwise' is not printed in your maths book. The end is West turned that number minus 2 right angles clockwise. Sample: if it is 3, then 3 − 2 = 1 right angle clockwise, and West ends at North. 9. Check: (c), (d) and (f) are full turns, so they end where they started. Answer: (a): South; (b): North; (c): East; (d): West; (e): East; (f): South; (g): the number is not printed; if it is 3, North.

Complete the table by filling the direction the children will face on completing the given turns. The starting direction is given in the table. $(a)$: North, two right angles clockwise; $(b)$: South, two right angles anti-clockwise; $(c)$: East, four right angles anti-clockwise; $(d)$: West, four right angles clockwise; $(e)$: North, $5$ right angles clockwise; $(f)$: South, $3$ right angles clockwise, $\frac{1}{2}$ right angle clockwise, $\frac{1}{2}$ right angle clockwise; $(g)$: West, $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ right angles clockwise, four $\frac{1}{2}$ right angles anti-clockwise

content.text:
1. The directions go clockwise: North, East, South, West. A right angle is a quarter turn, one step.
2. $(a)$: North, $2$ right angles clockwise: East, then South. It ends at South.
3. $(b)$: South, $2$ right angles anti-clockwise: East, then North. It ends at North.
4. $(c)$: East, $4$ right angles anti-clockwise: a full turn, back at East.
[Image: Fun with Turns: Ans1: solution]
5. $(d)$: West, $4$ right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at West.
6. $(e)$: North, $5$ right angles clockwise: $4$ of them are a full turn, and $5 - 4 = 1$ more takes it to East.
7. $(f)$: South, $3 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 4$ right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at South.
8. $(g)$: West. Four $\frac{1}{2}$ right angles are $2$ right angles anti-clockwise. The number before 'right angles clockwise' is not printed in your maths book. The end is West turned that number minus $2$ right angles clockwise. Sample: if it is $3$, then $3 - 2 = 1$ right angle clockwise, and West ends at North.
9. Check: $(c)$, $(d)$ and $(f)$ are full turns, so they end where they started.
Answer: $(a)$: South; $(b)$: North; $(c)$: East; $(d)$: West; $(e)$: East; $(f)$: South; $(g)$: the number is not printed; if it is $3$, North.
[Image: Fun with Turns: Ans1: solution (continued)]

(d): West, 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at West.
(e): North, 5 right angles clockwise: 4 of them are a full turn, and 5 − 4 = 1 more takes it to East.
(f): South, 3 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 4 right angles clockwise: a full turn, back at South.

Check: (c), (d) and (f) are full turns, so they end where they started.

content.text: Padma is facing the toy shop. What place will she face if she takes a half turn clockwise?
content.q_figure: A street seen from behind Padma, who faces the toy shop. A bookstall is on her left, a parking sign and a guard are on her right, and an ice cream cart is behind her.

content.text:
1. A half turn is $2$ quarter turns.
2. Padma faces the toy shop. On her right are the parking sign and the guard, on her left is the bookstall, and behind her is the ice cream cart.
3. Clockwise, the first quarter turn takes her to face the parking sign.
4. The second quarter turn takes her to face the ice cream cart.
[Image: Fun with Turns: Ans2: solution]
5. Check: a half turn makes her face the opposite way from the toy shop, and the ice cream cart is behind her.
Answer: The ice cream cart.
[Image: Fun with Turns: Ans2: solution (continued)]

topics.summary: A revision of the whole playground of turns: full and half turns, halves and quarters, angle names, eighths, sixths and twelfths, the minute hand, and clockwise and anti-clockwise.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked all round the playground of turns. Can you say one idea from each stop? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Full turn and half turn: a full turn brings you back to the starting position, and a half turn leaves you facing the opposite way.
3. Check: Sahana turns until her back is to the door. Is it a full turn or a half turn? A half turn.
4. Halves and quarters: 2 half turns make a full turn, 2 quarter turns make a half turn, and 4 quarter turns make a full turn.
5. Check: 1 half turn and 2 quarter turns make 1/2 + 2/4 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, a full turn.
6. Everyday objects turn only so far. Compare the greatest turn with a quarter turn: less, equal or more.
7. Angles arise from turns: a 1/4 turn is a right angle, less than a 1/4 turn is an acute angle, more than a 1/4 turn and less than a 1/2 turn is an obtuse angle, and a 1/2 turn is a straight angle. A 3/4 turn is more than a straight angle.
8. Check: a turn of 1/3 is more than 1/4 and less than 1/2. Which kind of angle is it? An obtuse angle.
9. Measuring turns: a circle in 8 parts gives 1/8 turns, with 2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2 and 6/8 = 3/4. A circle in 6 parts gives 1/6 turns, and half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn.
10. Check: how many 1/8 pieces make a quarter turn? 2 pieces, because 2/8 = 1/4.
11. Measuring angles: lay the pieces side by side and add their turns. 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, a right angle.
12. The minute hand makes a full turn in 60 minutes, so 15 minutes is a 1/4 turn and 5 minutes is a 1/12 turn.
13. Check: the minute hand moves 20 minutes. What turn is that? 20 × 3 = 60, so it is a 1/3 turn.
14. Clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move. The opposite is anti-clockwise.
15. Check: you face East and turn 2 right angles clockwise. Which direction do you face? East, then South, then West: you face West.

objectives.objective_text: Students name a turn as a full turn or a half turn by comparing where something faces with where it faced at the start.
Students name which child in the statue game made a full turn and which made a half turn, and explain the answer by comparing each child with the start.
Students find the turn made when half turns and quarter turns are joined in the same direction.
Students find the turn made when half turns and quarter turns are joined in the same direction on the giant wheel.
Students compare the greatest turn of an object with a quarter turn and say whether it is less than, equal to or more than a quarter turn.
Students join half turns and quarter turns on the wheel, and tick whether the greatest turn of an object is less than, equal to or more than a 1/4 turn.
Students name a turn from a fixed straw as a right, acute or obtuse angle by comparing it with a quarter turn.
Students name a half turn as a straight angle and a turn of 3/4 as more than a straight angle.
Students show acute and obtuse angles with a turning fan, and name right, acute, obtuse and straight angles in pictures.
Students show a turn on a circle folded into 8 equal parts and read it as a fraction of a full turn, such as 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2.
Students show 1/6 and 2/6 turns on a circle folded into 6 equal parts and show that half of a 1/6 turn is a 1/12 turn.
Students show and read turns of 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 3/8, 6/8 and 8/8, of sixths and of 1/12 on a disc, and find the starting arrow of a given turn.
Students measure an angle by laying turn pieces side by side on it and adding their fractions, and name the angle as acute, right or obtuse.
Students guess and check angles with turn pieces and read the turn an arrow makes.
Students draw an angle for a given turn by laying the pieces for that turn from a given line and drawing the second line along the last piece.
Students measure angles with turn pieces and then draw angles for given turns using the given lines.
Students find the turn the minute hand makes from the minutes it moves, find the minutes from the turn, and say where the hand stops.
Students find the turn or the minutes for each movement of the minute hand and mark where the hand stops.
Students tell whether a turn is clockwise or anti-clockwise by comparing it with the way the hands of a clock move.
Students find the direction faced after turns of right angles, clockwise or anti-clockwise, from North, East, South or West.
Students tick the direction of a quarter turn, fill in the ending direction after turns of right angles, and find the place faced after a half turn.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Can you recognise the child in the picture who has made a full turn? Who has made a half turn? How do you know? Discuss in class.
Book item: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction. It is like a ___ turn.
Book item: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. What happens if Reema takes 2 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn.
Book item: A giant wheel makes a full turn when it comes back to the starting position E. What happens if Reema takes 4 quarter turns in the same direction? It is like a ___ turn.
Book item: Write some of the everyday objects that involve turns. For example, taps, ___, ___, ___, ___, and ___.

Book item: What is the maximum possible turn in each of these cases? Check and tick: less than a 1/4 turn, 1/4 turn, or more than a 1/4 turn. (a): Clothes clip; (b): Door with hinge; (c): Tongs; (d): Scissors; (e): File cover
Book item: Do any of the objects in the table (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) make a half turn? Write their names.
Book item: Do any of the objects in the table (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) make a full turn? Write their names.
Book item: Use your paper fan to show different acute angles and obtuse angles.
Book item: Make an acute turn with the straws or fan. Continue to make another acute turn. Can the two acute turns together make another acute turn?

Book item: You might have built houses using the hard covers of notebooks or cardboard pieces. Look at the angles marked in the house. What angles are you able to see in this house? Write your answers as right, acute or obtuse angle. A: ___; B: ___; C: ___; D: ___; E: ___; F: ___; G: ___; H: ___
Book item: Make a 5-sided shape with 2 right angles, 2 obtuse angles, and 1 acute angle in your notebook.
Book item: Look at the angle formation between the legs of these gymnasts. Identify whether the angles are acute, obtuse, right or straight.
Book item: Show a 1/8 turn of the straw. Show a 2/8 turn. Show a 1/4 turn. Show a 3/8 turn.
Book item: What angle have you made with a 2/8 turn? A 1/8 turn is half of a quarter turn.
Book item: What angle have you made with a 4/8 turn?
Book item: Continue turning by 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, and 8/8. Check when you have completed a 3/4 turn and a full turn.
Book item: In the following circles, the end points of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns are shown. Draw arrows to show the starting points.
Book item: Show the turns of the straw equal to 1/6, 2/6, and so on until you complete a full circle.
Book item: Can you guess what turn of the straw will be equal to half of a 1/6 turn?

Book item: Guess the measures of each of the angles shown below. Then, check using your angle measuring tools. You may need to use a combination of measures. Also, state whether each of the angles is acute, right, or obtuse.

Book item: Guess the measure of the turns made by the arrow in each of the following cases. Verify with a combination of angle measuring tools. (a): 1/4 + 1/8 turn or 3/8 turn (this part is already solved in your maths book); (b): ___ turn; (c): ___ turn; (d): ___ turn

Book item: Measure each angle in the given shapes. Write the measure of the angles in terms of turns and describe whether they are acute, obtuse or right angles. (a): the lines AB and A'B' cross at C and B'A joins B' and A; angles marked at B' and A. (b): the four-sided shape D, E, D', E'; angles marked at D, E and D'. (c): the four-sided shape F, G, F', G'; angles marked at F, G and F'.
Book item: Draw angles for the given measures of turns using the given lines.
Book item: Draw the angles formed by the following turns in your notebook. 1/2 turn, 1/4 turn, 2/4 turn, 1/6 turn, 4/6 turn, 3/12 turn, 1/2 + 1/4 turn, and 1/8 + 1/6 turn.

Book item: Guess the measure of turns the minute hand of a clock makes in each of the following cases. The initial position of the minute hand is given. Draw the final position of the minute hand on the clock face. Discuss your reasoning in class. (a): When the minute hand moves by 15 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (b): When the minute hand moves by 30 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (c): When the minute hand moves by 45 minutes, it has made a ___ turn of the circle. (d): When the minute hand has turned by 1/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (e): When the minute hand has turned a full-circle, it has moved by ___ minutes. (f): When the minute hand has turned by 1/6 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes. (g): When the minute hand has turned by 4/12 of a full turn, it has moved by ___ minutes.

Book item: The creatures below have made a quarter turn once. Tick the direction in which they have moved. (a): ladybug (Clockwise/Anti-clockwise); (b): snail (Clockwise/Anti-clockwise); (c): bee (Clockwise/Anti-clockwise); (d): ant (Clockwise/Anti-clockwise)
Book item: Observe the direction of movement while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid or loosening a nut. Do they move clockwise or anti-clockwise?

Book item: The children in a class are playing a game in which the teacher tells them the direction in which they should rotate. Complete the table by filling the direction the children will face on completing the given turns. The starting direction is given in the table. (a): North, two right angles clockwise; (b): South, two right angles anti-clockwise; (c): East, four right angles anti-clockwise; (d): West, four right angles clockwise; (e): North, 5 right angles clockwise; (f): South, 3 right angles clockwise, 1/2 right angle clockwise, 1/2 right angle clockwise; (g): West, ___ right angles clockwise, four 1/2 right angles anti-clockwise
Book item: Padma is facing the toy shop. What place will she face if she takes a half turn clockwise?
Book item: What other way can Padma turn to face the same place?

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place on a school playground and its fair. Children turn on the spot, a giant wheel comes back to its starting seat, a straw and a paper fan turn, and a minute hand goes round. Turning shows what an angle is, how to name it and how to measure it as a part of a turn. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, turns, measures and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Seven tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.
points.title: Videos teach, tools explore

points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.
points.title: A tool in three steps

points.text: Every Let Us Do part, Let Us Think question, Fun with Turns question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.
points.title: Every book question has its own video

points.text: Every angle is shown as a start mark, a turning arm and the part of a full turn it has made. Angles are measured as parts of a full turn: halves, quarters, eighths, sixths and twelfths.
points.title: An angle is a turn

points.text: The pieces, the clock positions, the compass and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.
points.title: Only the book's numbers
